    Southwest Airlines Plus Card Review: Modest Benefits For A Low Annual Fee

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees).
    • In my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass.
    • Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees). In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card, which is Southwest Airlines’ lowest annual fee credit card.

    In my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass. I’ll also explain why other Southwest cards can be better, and share a great alternative to earning Southwest Rapid Rewards points altogether.

    Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card.

    Before I get into my Southwest Plus Card review, here are some of the key card details:.

    Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Plus Card’s pros and cons:.

    Let’s take a look at the Southwest Plus Card‘s welcome bonus, annual fee, and eligibility rules, as these are some of the most key factors to take into account if you’re considering applying.

    The Southwest Plus Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is one of the higher bonuses I’ve seen on this card recently, making now a particularly good time to apply.

    Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $960.

    Industry observers note that in terms of Southwest credit card eligibility, the card isn’t available to anyone who right now has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

    Beyond the restrictions related to which Southwest cards you have, keep in mind the general restrictions for Chase card approvals, including the 5/24 rule. However, there are increasing data points of this no longer being consistently enforced.

    Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

    For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

    In a recent development, you’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for this card now if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

    Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

    Industry observers note that this change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

    The Southwest Plus Card has a $99 annual fee, and you can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost.

    $99 is the lowest annual fee of any Southwest Airlines credit card. Looking at the high end, Southwest’s personal cards have annual fees of up to $229, and Southwest’s business cards have annual fees of up to $299.

    The Southwest Plus Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a solid card to use for purchases abroad.

    As far as the Southwest Plus Card‘s rewards structure goes, the card offers the following:.

    Since I value Southwest Rapid Rewards points at 1.2 cents each, I think you get an effective return of 2.4% on purchases that qualify for 2x points, and a 1.2% return on everything else.

    Industry observers note that it’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, though there are ultimately more rewarding cards out there for everyday spending. Plus, a few of the non-Southwest bonus categories have an annual cap, which limits how useful this card is for maximizing your return on gas station and grocery store purchases.

    I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Plus Card.

    Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

    Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

    Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

    According to recent reports, one great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

    According to recent reports, the Southwest Plus Card offers some benefits that could make the card worth keeping long term. However, this is also Southwest’s lowest annual fee card, so it doesn’t have the most benefits. What are the ongoing perks of having this card?

    According to recent reports, the Southwest Plus Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person. So with just one roundtrip flight per year, this benefit can almost offset the annual fee.

    Southwest now charges for seat selection, so it’s helpful that the Southwest Plus Card includes complimentary standard seat selection starting 48 hours out from departure. This perk is based on availability, and it could save you around $20 to $40 per flight.

    It has been revealed that another Southwest benefit is early boarding. You’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group. Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last.

    Each year on your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary, you’ll get a 10% promo code that applies to Southwest flights. Just note that this discount excludes Basic fares.

    In a recent development, on your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary every year, you’ll receive 3,000 bonus points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you’ll typically need 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book. In other words, those 3,000 Rapid Rewards points should get you around $36 worth of airfare on Southwest annually.

    According to recent reports, as part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

    This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Plus Card.

    According to recent reports, the Southwest Plus Card offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. Simply pay with your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for that amount.

    The Southwest Plus Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:.

    You’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

    One of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money.

    The Southwest Plus Card is a solid entry-level airline credit card. If you want a credit card from Southwest and want an annual fee as low as possible, then this card could make sense to you.

    Sources indicate that you’ll receive a 3,000-point bonus on your cardmember anniversary every year, and 25% savings on inflight purchases. The free checked bag benefit can save you $90 on a roundtrip and the complimentary standard seat selection benefit can add up quickly after a few flights. These perks can more than justify the annual fee, and that’s not even accounting for the massive welcome bonus.

    However, there are other options that I think can make more sense.

    If your main reason for considering the Southwest Rapid Rewards Plus Card is to earn points for Southwest award flights, you might be better off skipping a Southwest co-branded credit card altogether and just earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points. You can transfer Chase points to Southwest to book flights, and cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) have stronger earning categories and benefits overall.

    You can also redeem Ultimate Rewards points with other travel partners, not just Southwest, so this option gives you more flexibility.

    The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step up from the Southwest Plus Card, with a $149 annual fee. Here’s a look at its key perks:.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (learn more), the most premium personal Southwest card with a $229 annual fee. If you want as many Southwest perks as possible, this is a better pick.

    The Southwest Priority Card’s main perks include:.

    So you’re getting a higher return of 4.8% on Southwest spending on the Priority Card, based on my valuations, and better complimentary seat selection and upgrade options.

    In a recent development, if you want a Southwest Rapid Rewards business credit card in place of or in addition to a personal card, I highly recommend considering the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). The Southwest Performance Business Card offers the following benefits, which make it the best Southwest credit card, in my opinion:.

    The Southwest Performance Business Card offers a lot of points, and more perks overall than other Southwest cards.

    It has been revealed that the Southwest Plus Card is a good entry-level credit card for someone who wants to earn Rapid Rewards points without paying a high annual fee. It’s not the most valuable Southwest credit card in the lineup, but its benefits and strong welcome bonus make it a good option at this price point.

    Delta Is My Preferred Airline Of The “Big Three” US Carriers (Hear Me Out)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1405 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve never been one to take the easy road, so I thought I’d bite the bullet and talk about my love for Delta in what you might call a baptism of fire.
    • This year, Delta has nudged up to fourth most-flown of the 94 airlines I’ve tried out over the years, and I’d like to share a little bit about why.
    • In a recent development, starting from the ground, I am a substantial fan of what Delta is doing with its lounges.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’ve never been one to take the easy road, so I thought I’d bite the bullet and talk about my love for Delta in what you might call a baptism of fire. Before I jump in, I’m not here screaming that Delta is the best US airline. Far from it. Rather, I’m explaining why, as someone who is not based in the US, Delta is my go-to airline.

    This year, Delta has nudged up to fourth most-flown of the 94 airlines I’ve tried out over the years, and I’d like to share a little bit about why.

    In a recent development, starting from the ground, I am a substantial fan of what Delta is doing with its lounges. Stepping inside one of Delta’s newer Sky Clubs, you feel like you’re in the lobby bar of a luxury hotel rather than the corporate canteen-style spaces offered by competitors.

    I know these newer lounges aren’t in every airport yet — Honolulu (HNL) is a notable exception — but lately I’ve found myself enjoying them before the majority of my latest Delta flights departing from a US airport.

    Don’t get me started on the Delta One Lounges: I’ve visited locations at LAX and JFK, and these are without a doubt my favorite airline lounges in the US.

    Stepping onboard, I actually like the planes. In recent times, I’ve flown mainly on its Airbus A320 family aircraft, a few Boeing 757s (which I love), and once on a Boeing 767-300 from Honolulu to LAX.

    I like how they’ve all had seatback screens, I’ve never had an concern using my SkyMiles account to access the fast free WiFi (it’s decent, even though it’s not Starlink), and I’ve never felt uncomfortable on one of Delta’s planes.

    I also have to say, I’ve always had pleasant, if not better-than-your-average service when flying Delta.

    Recent findings suggest that I love a good redemption as much as the next frequent flyer. However, our credit cards in the UK earn us far fewer points than those in the US, so for me, redeeming points is the exception, not the norm.

    Recent findings suggest that as such, I don’t hate on Delta’s SkyMiles for its mostly sky-high redemption rates. Even if finding a one-way in Delta One from Rio or São Paulo to Fresh York for less than 470,000 miles is almost impossible.

    Besides, I credit my Delta flights to my Flying Blue account, which is therefore home to my SkyTeam elite status and miles earned on Delta and all other SkyTeam airlines.

    It has been revealed that neither do I fly often enough nor have the funds to unlock top-tier status in all three alliances. Aside from the Virgin Atlantic Gold status I got from a status match and my BA Silver, which expires in April, Flying Blue is the only program whose status I’m actively chasing.

    Sources indicate that as a direct result of Air France and KLM’s membership in the SkyTeam alliance, I actively choose to fly other SkyTeam airlines, such as Delta. Also, thanks to the relationship between Delta and fellow SkyTeam member Aeroméxico, I’ve managed to find great-value cash fares on several occasions when planning travel between Mexico and Canada or the US.

    Recent findings suggest that I actually used to be a die-hard American boy until the BA Club was sabotaged. In terms of lounges, aircraft comfort, complimentary amenities (like seat back screens and Wi-Fi), and service, Delta has felt like an upgrade.

    For what it’s worth, if status had nothing to do with it, I’d still choose Delta.

    Recent findings suggest that my experience with American, Delta, and United has mainly been on domestic flights around the US, including transcons. In fact, I’ve never flown Delta One, American Flagship, or United Polaris on long-haul international flights. Who knows, my top three could reshuffle once I’ve tried and tested each of those. Maybe I’ll have to have a word with Ben about this….

    Industry observers note that I know Delta gets a bad rep, but honestly I have only had pleasant experiences when flying the airline over the years. As long as I’m being loyal to SkyTeam, it will remain my preference when traveling to or around the US (unless it’s from the UK; then I’m team Virgin).

    It has been revealed that I’m going to make it a priority to fly each of American, Delta, and United’s best international long-haul products over the coming months. Watch this space for my thoughts on flying those for the first time, and to see whether Delta remains my US number one.

    I’m curious, what do you love or hate about Delta?

    #168445. When To Use The Flight Attendant Call Button (And When To Skip It)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1435 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    When To Use The Flight Attendant Call Button (And When To Skip It)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that to push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question.
    • It has been revealed that every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those).
    • The flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that to push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question. I’ll share my take, and then I’m curious to hear how OMAAT readers feel. Let’s start with some background, and then we’ll discuss best practices….

    It has been revealed that every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those). The flight attendant call button, is, as the name suggests, a way to call a flight attendant to your seat.

    The flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service. However, that’s not how all flight attendants interpret it, so I want to talk about that in a bit more detail.

    Sources indicate that in most of the world, the flight attendant call button seems to work as intended. It’s a useful way to call over a flight attendant, whether you want a drink refill, or there’s some sort of an emergency.

    Sources indicate that however, in the United States I’ve heard several flight attendants over the years announce that the call button is in fact the “emergency flight attendant call button,” advising passengers to only use it if absolutely necessary. Suffice to say that this kind of announcement isn’t approved by any airline.

    While people will often joke “well I’m happy you consider my drink request to be an emergency,” let’s talk about when it’s actually appropriate to use a flight attendant call button.

    Broadly speaking, it’s always appropriate to use the flight attendant call button for service in first & business class, especially on international airlines. You’re paying a premium for more service, and having an extra request on a long haul flight isn’t unreasonable.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ll take it a step further — at top airlines, crews generally prefer that you push the call button rather than going to the galley with your request. Foreign carriers typically have thick curtains between the galley and the cabin, and you generally shouldn’t try to go into the flight attendant’s “space” without permission. They’d much rather come to you. They might be putting on some makeup or eating a meal, and don’t want to be caught off guard. So absolutely push the flight attendant call button — it’s the courteous thing to do.

    It has been revealed that I do want to mention just one caveat — try to be respectful of the overall service flow. For example, if a cabin has 50+ business class seats and the crew is doing service with a cart and is currently in the aisle, wait until they finish that round of service before pushing the call button again, unless there’s something you absolutely need.

    When it comes to using the call button, you can’t beat Emirates first class, where you can voice or video call the crew with any requests, without them even having to come to your seat.

    It’s also interesting to observe the cultural differences between airlines when it comes to service approaches. For example, in Singapore Airlines first class I generally don’t push the flight attendant call button, since even on a long haul flight, a crew member seems to pass through the cabin every 10-15 minutes throughout the flight. The service is just so proactive that I don’t find it necessary.

    Industry observers note that cathay Pacific first class is exactly the opposite — the crews are spectacularly reactive. That might sound sarcastic, but it’s not. On Cathay Pacific you (hopefully) won’t see a flight attendant once between meal services without calling them, and that’s so that your privacy is maximized. But if you push the call button a flight attendant will cheerily appear within seconds.

    In a recent development, of course those are both airlines known for great service. You have all kinds of other airlines where flight attendants make a habit of not passing through the cabin, and when they do they almost seem to look down, to avoid making eye contact.

    Using the flight attendant call button in economy is trickier. There’s nothing inherently wrong with it, but the staffing ratio in economy is different than in first & business class, and in many cases flight attendants have to walk a lot further to your seat. Also keep in mind that on long haul flights the crew has rest periods, reducing the staffing ratio even further.

    Personally I think there’s nothing wrong with using the call button in economy:.

    Recent findings suggest that that being said, in economy I also think it’s more reasonable to stretch your legs and go to the galley yourself. Generally there’s a small setup with snacks and drinks, at least on long haul flights, so you can help yourself to that. Furthermore, in my experience flight attendants are typically “sitting in the open” more in economy than in business or first class, given that the volume of requests is greater.

    The above are my general thoughts, though is the story any different on airlines in the United States? This accounts for the fact that:.

    Industry observers note that on US airlines I’m generally a little more hesitant to use the call button. I see what kind of a vibe the crew gives me. In general I don’t mind pushing the call button in international first & business class on a US airline, while I avoid it on domestic flights. If I get the sense that the crew takes matter with use of the call button, I of course won’t use it.

    All airplane seats have individual flight attendant call buttons, though customs around using them seem to differ. In the United States, some flight attendants seem to think these buttons are just for emergencies, while outside the United States there are consistently no concerns with using them for service.

    Where do you stand on using the flight attendant call button, and what has your experience been?

    Who else ran to the comments to see how you crazy folk use the call button.

    I use it in business class if I'm done with a meal and am burried in the set table with plates and all. Without the call button the crew may not proactively come clear it for hours.

    In a recent development, if the airline offered complementary drinks, then no reason not to use it to ask for another. Just because they served you one doesn’t make a difference, there’s no cap on how many drinks are complementary so it’s part of the job. If the tray hasn’t been cleared and you need the bathroom. Yes you should feel comfortable calling the crew. If you want your meal early, that’s pushing it. You want an extra blanket? Maybe. You want to adjust the cabin temperature; I’d reserve this request for premium cabins, unless the temperature is ridiculous. Merely my opinion though, of course, now how it practically works - you will always get some cabin crew who don’t want to do extra work so even resent basic aspects of their job like serving drinks or clearing a table so you can, you know, get out of your seat to the bathroom - not really optional! I’m too hot/cold, I can’t wait to eat? Well that’s getting ridiculous. Even as a frequent F traveller I don’t expect them to rush a fine meal service just because I’m impatient. In an F cabin with say 3 other passengers, changing the cabin temperature should be done gracefully and only pushed back if other customers are opposing the request. I can see how this will play out totally differently in a cabin with 100 other passengers in close proximity.

    I do not care what cabin I’m travelling in, I’m pressing the button if I want something.

    According to recent reports, the flight attendants are there for my safety. And for my safety I need another gin and tonic.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that president Trump makes no secret of his desire to punish broadcasters whose content he dislikes.
    • How did we get to a point where the president and FCC chair can threaten a broadcaster’s license over disfavored content?
    • Rankin is an adjunct fellow with the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

    Sources indicate that president Trump makes no secret of his desire to punish broadcasters whose content he dislikes. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr is a willing partner, going so far as to threaten the licenses of Disney-owned ABC stations with an early renewal proceeding. This highly unusual move (purportedly for unlawful discrimination) followed President Trump’s demand that ABC and NBC affiliates lose their broadcast licenses for unfavorable coverage of him.

    How did we get to a point where the president and FCC chair can threaten a broadcaster’s license over disfavored content? Two features of federal law enable this abuse: a vague public interest standard open to broad, subjective interpretation, and an archaic equal time rule.

    Brian A. Rankin is an adjunct fellow with the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

    On “The Public Interest Demands Free Speech for Broadcasters”.

    GAO chief nominee triggers partisan clash at Senate hearing

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday.
    • Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.
    • “I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.

    “I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.

    Industry observers note that democrats have criticized Ueland, a longtime GOP Senate aide and administration official during both Trump terms, saying he is too politically biased to lead the nonpartisan watchdog agency which conducts investigations and audits for Congress. They also said Republicans ignored a law that Democrats say requires the convening of a special legislative commission to make recommendations for the post.

    It has been revealed that ueland mentioned if the Senate confirms him to lead the Government Accountability Office, “We can at the end of the day ... see a GAO which is more effective, which provides better information for Congress in a quicker way so Congress is able to take policy actions and drive change itself at this end of Pennsylvania Avenue.”.

    At the root of the partisan clash is a suspicion by Democrats that Trump is trying to install a puppet to lead an agency that has fought the administration repeatedly over the power of the purse and other matters.

    Democrats blasted Paul for rushing the hearing, which included a dozen other nominees for administration and judicial posts.

    Industry observers note that “It’s so apparent that this is a box-checking exercise,” stated Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the panel. “This committee is not doing due diligence, despite some of our members’ best efforts, because the chairman has chosen not to carry out his responsibility to provide advice and consent on nominations.”.

    In a recent development, democrats said Paul did not allow Peters to make an opening statement at the hearing and restricted the amount of time given to senators to ask questions. A GOP aide disputed this, noting that Paul did not give an opening statement himself, Peters arrived late and all senators were given five minutes to ask questions.

    According to recent reports, ueland has served as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the OMB director. Trump nominated Ueland to head the GAO, a legislative branch agency, Monday.

    Industry observers note that democrats noted that the GAO has concluded multiple times that the administration violated the law by "impounding," or refusing to spend, appropriated funds. OMB has argued that the GAO misread the law and that it does not have any authority over the executive branch.

    Peters told Ueland that the GAO had issued 12 reports accusing the administration of violating the law, and he asked if Ueland agreed.

    Ueland did not give a direct response.

    In a recent development, “First, many of those items indicated by those reports, I have not participated in,” he said. Ueland said he had not reviewed the reports that Peters provided to him earlier, and that he would not offer an opinion on them.

    He also said it was critical that he “not prejudge or come to this committee with informed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress.” Ueland said he has a “clear commitment to follow the process.”.

    Peters said when Ueland appeared before the committee last year after being nominated for the OMB post, he voiced support for the presidential authority of impoundment.

    “We’re going to expect you to continue to basically ignore Congress,” Peters remarked. “You’re going to be a rubber stamp for the administration.”.

    “That’s not so,” Ueland replied.

    Ueland remarked his experience as deputy overseeing the management side of OMB would be a “value add to GAO.” He cited his work “examining how the government actually functions, how it is organized, how it can be better optimized to deliver results.”.

    Sources indicate that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked Ueland how he would grade GAO’s work to date.

    Ueland mentioned he would give it a “medium grade over time.”.

    For example, he remarked GAO has 38 government operations on a “high-risk list … some of which have been on there for 36 years.”.

    By contrast, Ueland referred to his work at OMB, where he mentioned “you have seen a very swift and aggressive effort by this administration in this term to set up systems and processes to ensure that we are not sending money out the door that we shouldn’t.”.

    Paul asked Ueland what he would do if administration officials told him they did not like a GAO investigation or conclusion.

    Ueland mentioned he would “fully follow through on charges from Congress and in the event of obstacles figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information.” He said when he was a young staffer in the Senate, when there were disagreements between the legislative and executive branches, GAO and the administration had conversations “to see if there were appropriate paths forward.”.

    Responding to another question from Paul as to whether he would ignore a potential request from the White House to stop an investigation, Ueland said, “To be clear, yes.”.

    Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., who is seeking to be the ranking Republican on the committee in the next Congress, noted he was satisfied that Republicans followed the letter of the law requiring a commission to make recommendations to the president for comptroller general. He added that he was not “completely sure they have followed the entire spirit of the law.”.

    Sources indicate that “For me, personally, Mr. Ueland is a great candidate in this role for GAO,” Lankford said.

    Recent findings suggest that paul sent three recommendations for comptroller general, including Ueland, to the White House last week from the six Republican members of a 10-member bipartisan, bicameral commission. But he never convened the body to seek applications from and interview candidates for the post.

    And he gave the four Democrats on the commission less than 24 hours’ notice last week to offer their recommendations. Democrats charged that Paul subverted the process, and they did not offer recommendations.

    In a separate interview Wednesday, the president of the union that represents GAO employees decried the decision not to follow the commission process that characterized past comptroller general nominations.

    “We see that bipartisan process as extremely important to preserving and keeping the trust that GAO has with the entire Congress,” noted Benjamin Emmel, president of Local 1921 of the International Federation of Professionals and Technical Engineers.

    Emmel, a senior analyst at GAO, said by sidestepping that procedure, “there is a cloud that hangs above any nominee where one party dominates that process.”.

    He noted GAO’s credibility depends on members of both parties trusting that the organization is “nonpartisan, objective, independent and fair. If we lose that ability, we become less useful.”.

    According to recent reports, the union is not advocating for or against Ueland or any nominee for the office. The Homeland Security panel is not expected to vote on the nominations until after Thanksgiving.

    According to recent reports, the no annual fee Chase Freedom Unlimited® is one of Chase’s most compelling cards for everyday spending, especially if you’re willing to put in the effort to maximize value. The card offers 3% cash back (or 3x points) on dining, 1.5% cash back (or 1.5x points) on everyday spending, and there are ways to get significantly more value than that.

    I don’t want to bury the lede — if you collect Chase Ultimate Rewards points and use any personal Chase card other than the Chase Freedom Unlimited for your everyday spending, you’re not doing it right. The catch is that there’s a learning curve to using this card — for some people this will just be a good card, while for other people this will be an amazing card.

    This post is my in-depth Chase Freedom Unlimited review, so let’s take a look at all the details of the card, starting with the very basics.

    Link: Learn more about the Chase Freedom Unlimited®.

    Before I get into my detailed Chase Freedom Unlimited review, let me summarize some of the basics:.

    Here are my thoughts on the main Chase Freedom Unlimited pros and cons:.

    In a recent development, the Chase Freedom Unlimited is part of Chase’s “Freedom” card portfolio, and is an excellent complement to any of Chase’s cards earning Ultimate Rewards points. Before diving into all those details, let’s look at the Freedom Unlimited’s welcome bonus, eligibility, and fees, since those are obviously major factors people consider when applying for cards.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited at the moment has a welcome bonus whereby you can earn $200 cash back (20,000 points) after spending $500 within the first three months.

    Industry observers note that on the surface, points can be redeemed for one cent each, but you can potentially get a lot more value than that, as these points can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I value those at 1.7 cents each.

    Sources indicate that it’s worth mentioning that the Chase Freedom Unlimited comes with an introductory APR offer that breaks down into two parts: purchases and balance transfers. Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on purchases, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

    For balance transfers: Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on balance transfers, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

    Industry observers note that these intro APR periods can be useful, but just make sure you pay off your entire balance before the offer ends. Otherwise, you’ll be stuck paying a high interest rate, which defeats the purpose.

    Eligibility for the Chase Freedom Unlimited is unrelated to eligibility for any other Chase cards, so you could earn the bonus on this card and the Freedom Flex Card, etc. The Chase Freedom Unlimited is not available to those who currently have the card, or those who have received a newly introduced cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months.

    Chase’s general credit card application rules, such as 5/24, generally apply, though that rule isn’t necessarily consistently enforced anymore.

    According to recent reports, there’s not a published credit score you need to get approved for the Freedom Unlimited, though I’d hope to have a score in the good to excellent range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, which is unbeatable. You can also add authorized customers to the card for no fee, so you can accrue rewards for their spending as well as your own. Obviously that’s a major upside of the card.

    While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a fantastic card for purchases within the United States, it does have 3% foreign transaction fees, so I don’t recommend using this card abroad.

    If you’re looking for a great card with no foreign transaction fees, consider the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) or Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more).

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited has an awesome rewards structure, which not only includes an excellent return on everyday spending, but also includes some valuable bonus categories.

    Before we get into this, note that in each case the percentage cash back can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points, at a rate of one cent per point. I’ll talk more below about how that’s possible, but that’s really how you maximize value with the card.

    It has been revealed that the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 5% cash back on travel purchased through Chase Travel℠ (or potentially 5x Ultimate Rewards points). Purchases made outside the Chase travel portal will earn 1.5% cash back (or 1.5 Ultimate Rewards points per dollar).

    Industry observers note that the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back on dining, including takeout and delivery (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is great for a no annual fee card, as this essentially makes this one of the best credit cards for dining spending.

    It has been revealed that the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back at drugstores (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is an awesome bonus, since drugstores isn’t a category where you otherwise see many cards offering bonuses.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday spending (or potentially 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points). The 1.5% cash back return isn’t that exciting, given that other cards offer 2% cash back. What is valuable, however, is the ability to earn 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent, as there’s no better Chase card for everyday spending.

    Personally I value Chase points at 1.7 cents each, so to me the card offers the equivalent of a 2.55% return on everyday spending.

    Recent findings suggest that the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday purchases, and 3-5% cash back in select bonus categories. On the surface, those rewards are really straightforward, as you can redeem the cash back for statement credits, a direct deposit in an eligible Chase account, for gift cards, or for travel booked through Chase Travel. You can even redeem your cash back toward Amazon purchases, though at the rate of 0.8 cents per point (so please don’t redeem that way!!).

    However, if you’re looking to earn travel rewards, you can get a significantly better return on spending than that.

    In a recent development, while the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a cash back card, in reality the card earns Ultimate Rewards points. You earn 1.5x points per dollar spent, and then ordinarily each point can be redeemed for one cent cash back. That’s how Chase arrives at the valuation of 1.5% cash back with the card.

    Sources indicate that however, if you have the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with another card that earns “premium” Ultimate Rewards points, then you can do significantly better. These cards include the following:.

    According to recent reports, with one of those cards, suddenly your points are much more valuable. Transferring points between cards is easy and can be done online. You can learn more about that process in this post.

    Personally, the way I like to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is to transfer them to airline and hotel partners, which include the following:.

    This can be the best way to redeem points toward premium travel experiences. If you want to redeem for first or business class travel or stay at luxury hotels, this option is for you.

    It has been revealed that one thing worth noting is that Chase recently devalued the transfer ratio to World of Hyatt to 4:3 for the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred. You’ll need the Chase Sapphire Reserve or Sapphire Reserve for Business to get the full 1:1 transfer rate with Hyatt. No matter which of these cards you have, points transfer to all other partners at a 1:1 ratio.

    While my favorite way to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is through the transfer partners, there are also ways to redeem Chase points at an advantageous rate toward travel purchased through Chase Travel℠:.

    That increases the value of your points by up to 100% right there.

    Sources indicate that for a no annual fee card, the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers a solid selection of benefits and purchase protection, which cardmembers will certainly appreciate. Let’s cover those, though let me of course remind everyone to always check the guide to benefits for the latest terms & conditions associated with these perks.

    According to recent reports, with the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you can extend the time period of your United States manufacturer’s warranty by an additional year on eligible warranties of three years or less. If you’re making an expensive purchase, this could save you a huge amount.

    Sources indicate that with the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you’re covered for new purchases for 120 days against damage or theft of up to $500 per item, and up to $50,000 per account. Again, this makes the card an excellent option for everyday spending, given how much money purchase protection can save you.

    In a recent development, the Chase Freedom Unlimited will reimburse cardmembers up to $1,500 per covered traveler and $6,000 per trip on prepaid fares that can’t be cancelled if your trip is canceled or cut short by sickness or another covered reason. More premium cards have more travel protections and higher limits, but this is pretty nice for a no annual fee cash back card.

    Industry observers note that with Chase Credit Journey, you get unlimited access to your credit score and more. This is free for Chase customers, including those who have the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

    One of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money, and having the Chase Freedom Unlimited gives you access to that.

    With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you get six months of complimentary DashPass membership. Note that when you take advantage of this, you’ll be auto-enrolled in a paid DoorDash strategy after six months, at the rate of $9.99 per month. So you’ll want to be sure you cancel before the complimentary plan expires, assuming you don’t value it.

You get up to $10 off non-restaurant DoorDash orders each quarter, up to $40 a year. This perk is presently valid for enrollment through December 31, 2027.

    It has been revealed that the Chase Freedom Unlimited qualifies for 2% cash back on Lyft purchases made through the app — a 0.5% bonus on top of the card’s standard earning rate. This promotion runs through September 30, 2027.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited is one of the all around best cards for everyday spending. It’s a credit card that I have, and it’s one that I think is worth holding onto.

    According to recent reports, if you’re in the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem and put everyday spending on cards in the portfolio, then picking up the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a must. However, the key is to have the card in conjunction with a card earning premium Ultimate Rewards points — the Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Ink Business Preferred, or Sapphire Reserve for Business — so that you’re really maximizing your rewards.

    According to recent reports, I can’t emphasize enough that having the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with either the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve is probably the best card combo you can have.     The cards otherwise have overlapping bonus categories, like offering 3x points on dining and drugstores, etc. Personally I think both cards are worth having. If I could just have one, though, I’d probably choose the Freedom Unlimited, since it’s better for everyday spending.

    Chase has two “Unlimited” cards — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (learn more). These cards are very similar — both have no annual fee, and both offer 1.5x points (the Ink Unlimited on business purchases). So, what’s the difference?

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited is a key card to maximizing your overall Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, in conjunction with the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve.

    According to recent reports, the Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, and offers a minimum of 1.5x points per dollar spent. Let me make my advice as concise as possible here: if you have the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve, then you absolutely should have the Freedom Unlimited, so you’re maximizing your return on everyday, non-bonused Chase spending.

    Park Hyatt Dubai Reopening In 2027, After Full Renovation: First Look At Latest Rooms

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed, so that it could undergo a renovation.
    • The hotel is expected to reopen in the spring of 2027, and the first pictures of the newly introduced room product have just been revealed, as flagged by rota.
    • Dubai is a city that has endless hotels at all price points.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed, so that it could undergo a renovation. That was probably good timing, given the massively decreased demand we’ve seen for travel to the United Arab Emirates this year.

    The hotel is expected to reopen in the spring of 2027, and the first pictures of the newly introduced room product have just been revealed, as flagged by rota. Let’s take a look at those details, but first, I’d like to briefly talk about why I have a soft spot for this property.

    Dubai is a city that has endless hotels at all price points. I don’t have a single favorite hotel in the city, as it really depends on so many factors, from what you’re willing to pay, to the area you want to be in, to how substantial you want the property to be, to what you value most.

    In a recent development, after all, the concept of hotels in Dubai is a bit different than in other cities, given that alcohol is primarily only served at restaurants in hotels. As a result, hotels are very much the social scenes, both for guests and non-guests.

    Anyway, the 223-key Park Hyatt Dubai opened all the way back in 2005, and I can’t count how many times I’ve stayed there over the years, going back to just shortly after it initially opened. There’s a lot to like about the resort:.

    To me, it very much fits into the category of being an urban resort, in terms of being a destination, while having ideal proximity to things.

    According to recent reports, there are just some hotels where you have such fond memories for a variety of reasons, and for me, the Park Hyatt Dubai is definitely among them. In part, maybe it can’t help but remind me of the “good old days” of redeeming Alaska Mileage Initiative miles for Emirates first class.

    Industry observers note that remember being able to redeem 100,000 Alaska miles for Emirates first class from the US to basically anywhere in the world via Dubai, with a free stopover there, and no carrier imposed surcharges? And that says nothing of being able to fly from the US to London with a stopover in Mauritius, and layovers in Dubai twice on a one-way (IYKYK). 😉.

    According to recent reports, in May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed for the main portion of its renovation. If you go to the hotel’s website, you’ll see the following restrictions:.

    Park Hyatt Dubai is right now closed as it embarks on a defining transformation – a moment of careful, considered renewal in pursuit of an experience that is more refined, more exceptional, and more authentically itself than ever before.

    Behind the scenes, every space and every detail is being thoughtfully elevated – honouring the quality and commitment to luxury hospitality that have made this sanctuary on Dubai Creek so singular, while reimagining the perfect stay.

    With an anticipated reopening date of Q1 2027, we look forward to sharing more updates as that moment approaches, and to welcoming you back to a truly reawakened Park Hyatt Dubai. Because true elegance never stands still. It evolves – and in evolving, it is perfected.

    According to recent reports, as it at the moment stands, the hotel is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. Now, the hotel is accepting villa reservations as of January 1, 2027, but that’s separate from the main part of the hotel. We’ve known that everything about the hotel would change, but not many renderings had been shared up until now.

    One thing is for sure — there’s no denying that the rooms were in desperate need of a renovation, given that they hadn’t undergone any meaningful updates since the hotel first opened.

    It has been revealed that the hotel has now updated its website to show pictures of the latest room product, and you can find those renderings below. I’m conflicted here. On the one hand, this looks much more luxurious than the old setup. On the other hand, the design just looks incredibly generic, and like it could be anywhere. I wish we’d see a little more sense of place.

    On the plus side, the hotel’s grounds and general bones otherwise have a decent sense of place, so I hope that’s at least maintained with the updates.

    According to recent reports, leadership at the Park Hyatt Dubai had been vocal about how they hope to charge much higher rates after the renovation. I think it’s safe to say that’s all up in the air, based on how the situation in the Middle East evolves. As things right now stand, I see entry level rates in April that are $600+, while I see the lowest rates in summer at $350+.

    I feel like that pricing is very much on the optimistic side, but again, there are lots of moving parts with the Middle East hotel situation.

    In a recent development, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed in May 2026, and is right now undergoing a full renovation. In recent years we’ve seen a newly introduced beach club and new dining outlets added, but this should be by far the most meaningful patch since the hotel opened over two decades ago.

    The hotel is expected to fully reopen in April 2027, and the new rooms look like a huge improvement in terms of how luxurious they are. However, there’s definitely a sense of place missing, so I’m curious how the overall design evolves.

    What do you make of the changes coming to the Park Hyatt Dubai?

FWIW once it reopens, free tools like Arbitrica or similar check the same hotel from dozens of countries to find kind of the lowest price on Earth, since rates and inventory vary by country. I'd wait for the first reviews before booking April anyway.

    Hopefully, they fixed the low curbed walk in showers that leaked all over the bathroom.

    This is the whole ballgame: “given the massively decreased demand we’ve seen for travel to the United Arab Emirates this year.” Yeah, it’s not just UAE; it’s the whole region.     Tech Report: Three Women Argued Over An American Airlines Delay—Then Got Kicked Off And Blamed For Missed Connections

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that three women were escorted off an American Airlines flight from Knoxville to Charlotte on Saturday night after an argument with a flight attendant, costing passengers their connections.
    • Retired Kansas City Royals vice president Mike Swanson called them “princesses” in his story of the November 21 incident.
    • Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that three women were escorted off an American Airlines flight from Knoxville to Charlotte on Saturday night after an argument with a flight attendant, costing passengers their connections. Retired Kansas City Royals vice president Mike Swanson called them “princesses” in his story of the November 21 incident. The plane was already late getting to Knoxville, before the women could have held it up. Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026 In a follow-up on Twitter, Swanson explains that one woman complained to the flight attendant about how long it had taken to board. The flight attendant told the women they were ready to depart and to fasten their seat belts. The exchange escalated: The three got loud and the attendant wasn’t having it. They gone. Video shows two women walking toward the front with their belongings, followed by a uniformed officer. Swanson says three were removed. He says several passengers missed connections in Charlotte. Yelling at a flight attendant because your flight is late is a lousy strategy for getting home sooner. Last year I wrote about an American Airlines passenger who told a flight attendant to shut up during the safety demonstration and wound up getting the plane sent back to the gate. It appears this was American Eagle flight 5675 on November 21, operated by PSA Airlines using a Bombardier CRJ900, registration N557NN. That flight was scheduled to leave Knoxville at 8:04 p.m. and arrive in Charlotte at 9:28 p.m. It took off at 9:57 p.m. and landed at 10:34 p.m. Charlotte is a particularly bad place to lose your connection buffer. I’ve written about how arriving on a regional jet can mean waiting for a valet checked bag and then making a long walk from Concourse E. A late evening arrival also leaves fewer chances to recover with another flight that night. However, that aircraft’s inbound flight from Charlotte didn’t land in Knoxville until 8:35 p.m. It was supposed to have arrived at 7:34 p.m. The plane was still arriving 31 minutes after it should have departed on its next trip. The women weren’t responsible for the original delay. Removing them may have used up whatever chance remained to make his connection, but we don’t whether he’d have made it without the argument.     #168437. Tech Report: American Airlines Loses O’Hare Gate Appeal—But United’s Plan To Drive It Out Of Chicago Is Failing

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 31m • 📚 Deep Dive (6165 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: American Airlines Loses O’Hare Gate Appeal—But United’s Plan To Drive It Out Of Chicago Is Failing

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines just lost its appeal to undo Chicago O’Hare’s gate reshuffle.
    • The new ruling upholds the refusal to issue a preliminary injunction.
    • I still think American has the better argument about the contract.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines just lost its appeal to undo Chicago O’Hare’s gate reshuffle. But it’s already bought two gates from Spirit, earned back gate space through its own growth, and survived United’s effort to push it out of Chicago. The airline’s position is stronger than when it sued, and judges haven’t finally decided whether the city broke its contract. The newly introduced ruling upholds the refusal to concern a preliminary injunction. The question of whether Chicago took American’s gates too early, after promising to give the airline a chance to grow into additional space first still hasn’t been resolved. I still think American has the better argument about the contract. I’ve also been skeptical from the beginning that they’d get an injunction, since money damages seemed possible. The November 19 appellate decision fits that distinction, although the trial judge’s preliminary reading of the contract was unfavorable to American. The judge accepted that Chicago made American an explicit promise The dispute goes back to the 2018 airport lease. United was getting gates freed up by Delta’s move to Terminal 5. American objected to widening United’s advantage, and Chicago agreed to three additional gates on the north side of the L concourse extension. The lease called for gate assignments following an attached map, with those assignments remaining in place for at least twelve months. American’s argument was that it needed to actually receive the promised capacity before that protected period could run. Otherwise United could grow using its additional gates while American waited for its own, and then the city would use the unequal flying to take gates away from American. The way gates work at Chicago O’Hare is that prior flying determines future gate space (or, technically, ‘linear frontage’). That’s the problem I identified when American first filed its lawsuit. The timing was part of the bargain that got American to support the redevelopment agreement in the first place. And the trial judget accepted that the city and American had agreed to tie the process to the three additional gates becoming operational: For purposes of this motion, that much—the Court has no doubt—was the deal. His position, though, is that the city’s fingers were crossed, suggesting that the explicit written commitment didn’t make it into the final lease, or at least that American couldn’t establish that it had: The language identifies completion of the Terminal 5 expansion and an airline’s relocation there as the triggers. It doesn’t separately name completion of American’s three gates. The additional gates appear on the map as common use space, which the city controls, rather than space reserved for American’s preferential use. The lease states it’s the complete agreement. The judge treated its language as unambiguous and excluded the earlier negotiations as a way to add a condition to it. American’s last additional gate became operational March 14, 2025. Under its reading, the protected year therefore ran through March 2026, and the next redetermination could begin April 1, 2027. Chicago instead treated the protected period as having begun in December 2023, allowing redistribution in 2025. The city’s reading is silly. The map is part of the signed agreement. Requiring the city to deliver the capacity shown there before starting a year of protected assignments doesn’t require inventing a promise outside the contract. And designating a gate common use doesn’t explain how a gate that isn’t operational can fulfill a promise intended to let an airline ramp up flying. Why American lost the injunction appeal The appellate court assumed American could satisfy the initial requirements for an injunction and still concluded that the harm from blocking the gate changes justified denying one. It was reviewing whether the trial judge abused his discretion, NOT deciding the contract dispute from scratch. American’s problem was that it didn’t establish losing the gates would destroy its Chicago hub. It planned to operate the same number of flights using fewer gates, with more flying at less attractive times and less room to recover from delays. That could cost money, make operations worse and harm passengers but it made the injury look measurable. That was my original point – that this would be a case for future damages rather than an injunction. Meanwhile, the other airlines had planned schedules around the redistribution. United projected more than 2,000 cancellations if it were blocked. That number was overblown but the court accepted that changing the arrangements would disrupt passengers, other airlines, and airport construction. And the expectation that American would win gates back in the next allocation (which it did) undercut the argument that it faced an irreversible decline. Timing hurt American, too. Chicago announced the redistribution in February 2025. American sued in May but didn’t request preliminary relief until July. By the September hearing, the October gate changes were imminent and preparations were well underway. American argued that the city shouldn’t get to invoke the hardships from correcting an agreement they deliberately broke. The appeals court rejected that approach because it saw a reasonable dispute over what the contract meant. In my view, Chicago (intentionally) muddied the contract issue enough to make it less clear. This decision doesn’t end American’s lawsuit. It upholds the denial of a preliminary injunction. The contract claims and potential damages are still unresolved. The court rejected the argument that implementation of the gate changes had made the appeal moot, since a court could still order an effective remedy. United’s strategy ran into the airport’s actual capacity Chicago seemed strongly inclined to help its hometown airline. United’s headquarters are valuable to the city, especially with rumors of a move to Denver hanging over the relationship. My coverage of the gate dispute even generated an angry phone call from Chicago “shadow mayor” Jason Lee. United saw a chance to turn American’s slow recovery from the pandemic into a permanent retreat. American had retired too many aircraft and couldn’t rebuild everywhere at once. Fewer Chicago departures meant fewer gates, which could make future growth harder. United CEO Scott Kirby tried to create pressure by talking up American’s Chicago losses and getting financial analysts to question why it should stay. United then announced additional flying on the morning of American’s earnings call, practically writing the questions for them. This was strategic flying. United clearly didn’t want all of that additional capacity. It wanted invesors to believe that any growth would be matched, so American couldn’t improve its gate position and would just lose more money trying. Kirby told analysts United would add “as many flights as are required” to protect its gate count. Then the Federal Aviation Administration intervened. The airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines were filing, especially with construction constraining movement on the ground. Its summer order capped scheduled arrivals and departures at 2,708 per day from May 17 through October 24. The government used approved summer 2025 schedules as its baseline. It rejected rewarding airlines for filing unrealistic 2026 schedules to improve their negotiating position. United’s much larger proposed buildup didn’t entitle it to preserve that bigger share while forcing American to shrink. The government effectively called United’s bluff. The cap limited American, too, but it protected the existing competitive balance against United’s attempt to overwhelm it with additional flights. American had also grown enough during 2025 to earn back gate space in October’s redistribution. The returned space amounts to roughly three narrowbody gate equivalents. Separately, American acquired Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases for $30 million, which I was first to report. That reduces the practical stakes of this appeal, but it still seems that Chicago broke its agreement to benefit United. American needs Chicago to rebuild the business Kirby claims American loses so much money in Chicago that it should leave. Some version of those losses are real, created in part by the undersized schedule it had been flying. But the size and meaning of the losses get overstated. It requires assigning headquarters overhead to the hub that doesn’t disappear if the hub closes. And American would lose connecting traffic and credit card customers if that happened, too. American needs to be relevant in the largest markets where people spend heavily on cards. Retreating from Chicago would make AAdvantage less valuable to Chicago customers, and make its Citibank cards harder to sell and less attractive to spend on. Attributing credit card revenue to the customers and markets that generate it produces a different picture than spreading that revenue across flights throughout the network. That’s why Chicago belongs alongside American’s efforts to rebuild Los Angeles as gates return after construction, and its looks to bring Alaska Airlines into its Atlantic and Pacific joint ventures. They’re working to regain relevance in the largest spend markets in the country. The Chicago fight has also given employees something to rally around. In the post-earnings employee meeting I covered in January, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called United the “common enemy” and made it out to be a battle for loyalty and credit card performance. He reported roughly 20% growth in loyalty enrollments, card acquisitions, and local market share over the preceding nine months. Requiring the city to deliver the capacity shown there before starting a year of protected assignments doesn’t require inventing a promise outside the contract. And designating a gate common use doesn’t explain how a gate that isn’t operational can fulfill a promise intended to let an airline ramp up flying.

    Aeromexico 787s Get Makeover With Newly introduced Business Class, Premium Economy

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s.
    • Recent findings suggest that I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly revealed at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero.
    • To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet right now consists of 25 planes, including:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

    Recent findings suggest that I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly revealed at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero. However, the airline has now released a video on social media with additional details, so I’d like to publish an revision to reflect that.

    To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet right now consists of 25 planes, including:.

    Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was declared by the company’s CEO at last week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that the initiative is for the 787-9s to get all-newly introduced cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

    Sources indicate that the 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the cabins will be updated between 2029 and 2031, so that’s between three and five years from now (and that assumes no additional delays).

    Sources indicate that we’ll talk more about the upcoming business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

    The plane will also have 69% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the upcoming premium economy cabin.

    It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

    Sources indicate that aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

    Aeromexico has published the below video about its all-new cabins, which gives you a sense of what we can expect.

    A post shared by Aeroméxico (@aeromexico).

    For those who don’t want to watch the video, below are some screen grabs.

    Side note — is this new, or has Aeromexico been doing a cute tequila service for a long time?!? If I knew Aeromexico was serving shots, I would’ve prioritized the airline much higher on my list of products to review. 😉.

    Industry observers note that while details are otherwise limited, we know that Aeromexico’s fresh Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new seat. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

    I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

    It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

    Aeromexico is planning some massive upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

    As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out between 2029 and 2031, so unfortunately patience will be required.

    #168435. Hakeem Jeffries’s Reckless Medicare Expansion

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (552 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    Hakeem Jeffries’s Reckless Medicare Expansion

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that we have long warned that if Republicans did not get serious about advancing their own vision for health care, Democrats would use their next opportunity to further expand the role of government.
    • In a recent development, fresh off a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries made a radical proposal.
    • No doubt, with a stampede of upcoming socialists joining his caucus, Jeffries is trying to get ahead of the left-wing push for a fully government-run system branded as “Medicare for All.” When last nationally debated in 2019, it was estimated to add $34 trillion to existing federal spending with no plausible financing mechanism.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that we have long warned that if Republicans did not get serious about advancing their own vision for health care, Democrats would use their next opportunity to further expand the role of government. And here we are.

    In a recent development, fresh off a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries made a radical proposal. He endorsed lowering the retirement age of Medicare and adding vision, hearing, and dental coverage to the program. Additionally, he remarked that the government should provide coverage for all children.

    No doubt, with a stampede of upcoming socialists joining his caucus, Jeffries is trying to get ahead of the left-wing push for a fully government-run system branded as “Medicare for All.” When last nationally debated in 2019, it was estimated to add $34 trillion to existing federal spending with no plausible financing mechanism.

    At this point, Jeffries’s proposal is theoretical. There’s a substantial budgetary difference between lowering the Medicare eligibility age from its current 65 to 60, and lowering it to 50 — as Senator Kirsten Gillibrand and other senators are proposing. There are also questions about what sort of premiums, if any, would be required for near-retirees to “buy in” to the program or how generous the theoretical vision, hearing, and dental benefits would be. Filling in those blanks is the difference between a proposal that costs a few hundred billion dollars and one that costs trillions of dollars.

    But it’s preposterous at this stage to start any discussion of Medicare with a suggestion that spending on the program needs to be increased rather than reined in — especially to cover a population without a high uninsured rate. Over the next decade, the federal government is projected to spend $18.5 trillion on Medicare, making it the largest expenditure apart from that other federal entitlement, Social Security. Medicare no longer collects enough money in payroll taxes to cover current benefits, let alone added benefits that cover more people. Even a more modest lowering of the retirement age to 60 would add over 7 million beneficiaries. On its current trajectory, Medicare’s trust fund (the money it is “owed” by the rest of the government from the days when it was running surpluses) would be exhausted by 2033.

    Industry observers note that medicare is a major driver of the nation’s broader fiscal problem. Already, debt held by the public has eclipsed 100 percent of gross domestic product. By the end of the decade, it is projected to reach 120 percent. By comparison, debt peaked at 106 percent during World War II. Now we are on track to exceed that number, not during a global crisis, but during an ordinary period of relative peace and prosperity. And that’s before Jeffries grabs the gavel with a massive majority behind him.

    Perhaps more concerning, President Trump indicated last week that he may be game for some compromise proposal. “There is a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on health care,” he said.

    If Trump is serious and actually considers cutting a deal with Democrats to expand Medicare, congressional Republicans should fight it at all costs.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    On “Hakeem Jeffries’s Reckless Medicare Expansion”.
