    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, new York Kennedy Airport (JFK) is currently undergoing a $19 billion modernization. While this includes all kinds of updates, the two biggest developments are the opening of two new terminals — we’re talking about Terminal 6 and Terminal One (not to be confused with Terminal 1).

    As you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time. Per the latest updates, the expectation is that Terminal 6 will open before the end of 2026, while Terminal One will open in the first quarter of 2027.

    Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.

    JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open with a phased approach as of December 2026. To cover the very basics:.

    The below video of the terminal should give you a good sense of what to expect in terms of the passenger experience, so I’d recommend checking that out.

    It has been revealed that all things considered, this new terminal moving is awesome, given the quality of terminals at JFK otherwise. For those originating or terminating in New York, this should be ideal. For those connecting to or from JetBlue in Terminal 5, this will also make connections much easier. Meanwhile for a limited number of other passengers, this might make connections a bit more complicated, for cases where airlines are moving away from their partners (like Cathay Pacific moving from American’s Terminal 8 to Terminal 6).

    In a recent development, roughly 17 airlines are expected to eventually operate out of JFK Terminal 6, though that will happen in two phases. Broadly speaking, we’ll see some JetBlue operations move there (since the airline is a core tenant), and on top of that, we’ll largely see airlines move from Terminal 1, Terminal 7, and Terminal 8.

    So the expectation is that the following airlines will eventually operate from JFK Terminal 6:.

    Recent findings suggest that there is still a bit of a mystery as to the order in which airlines will move to JFK Terminal 6. For one, there’s the two phases of the terminal opening, but even within each phase, it won’t fully be overnight.

    We know that All Nippon Airways, Cathay Pacific, Condor, Frontier, Lufthansa Group carriers, and TAP Air Portugal, will move in the first phase. Meanwhile we know that Air India will move in the second phase. But for the remainder of the airlines, there’s a lack of certainty on that front.

    Recent findings suggest that now, we’ll see if this sticks, and how accurate it is, but current schedule filings suggest that Condor will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 3, while Cathay Pacific will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 15 (thanks to Peter_ for flagging this). So it sounds like we could potentially be just over a week from the first airline moving, which would be awesome!

    It has been revealed that in terms of lounges, we have confirmation that Terminal 6 will have outposts from Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, Aer Lingus, and Air India. Hopefully the upcoming lounges are ready to go as airlines make the move, but I wouldn’t consider that to be a sure thing, given the complexity of airport operations.

    The Air India lounge definitely won’t open anytime soon, since the airline is only moving in the second phase. Meanwhile the Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus lounges, will hopefully open soon(ish). Of course I’m most excited to see what Cathay Pacific has in store, given its amazing lounge quality.

    It has been revealed that JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open before the end of 2026, and if current filings are to be believed, the move could happen as soon as early December. It appears that Condor and Cathay Pacific might be among the first airlines to move, so hopefully Cathay Pacific’s newly introduced lounge isn’t too far behind. So we’ll mark this as “developing,” but the completion of the first exciting phase of this $19 billion project is imminent.

    #168431. Etihad Rolls out U.S. Credit Cards With Elite Status—But Most Americans Should Skip Them

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Etihad Rolls out U.S. Credit Cards With Elite Status—But Most Americans Should Skip Them

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
    • credit cards, including a $499 card that offers Gold status after a single Etihad purchase.
    • According to recent reports, qatar Airways status that comes the first year with their premium card can get you into American Airlines and Alaska Airlines lounges on domestic trips (and American Airlines international business class lounge access).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

    Etihad has rolled out two U.S. credit cards, including a $499 card that offers Gold status after a single Etihad purchase. That’s the sort of benefit that usually gets my attention. But I wouldn’t recommend either card to most U.S. consumers.

    According to recent reports, qatar Airways status that comes the first year with their premium card can get you into American Airlines and Alaska Airlines lounges on domestic trips (and American Airlines international business class lounge access). Emirates status lets you book first class awards that non-status members can’t. Etihad’s status doesn’t do either of those things, and you can earn their miles faster with other cards.

    The two cards launched November 20 through First National Bank of Omaha. They’re Etihad’s first U.S. cobrands, with annual fees of $99 and $499.

    Here are the main differences in the offers: Benefit   Etihad Guest Visa Signature   Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature Annual fee   $99   $499 Initial bonus   40,000 miles: 10,000 after first purchase, plus 30,000 after $3,000 in spending within the first three billing cycles   60,000 miles: 20,000 after first purchase, plus 40,000 after $7,000 in spending within the first three billing cycles Etihad purchases   3 miles per dollar   5 miles per dollar Partner airline purchases   2 miles per dollar   3 miles per dollar Other purchases outside the U.S. 2 miles per dollar   2 miles per dollar Other U.S. purchases   1 mile per dollar   1 mile per dollar The initial offers require applying by February 3, 2027. Both cards waive foreign transaction fees. The Premier card also includes Priority Pass, a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee credit every four years, and 3,000 miles after the first Etihad purchase and at each card anniversary. The status rules are: $99 card: Silver after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days. Keep Silver with $20,000 in annual card spending or $3,000 in Etihad purchases. $499 card: Silver at account opening, then Gold after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days. Keep Gold with $40,000 in annual card spending or $8,000 in Etihad purchases. Otherwise, you get Silver. Both earn one tier mile per dollar spent. The cheaper card caps this at 25,000 tier miles per calendar year, while Premier has no cap. These are status credits, separate from the miles you redeem for travel. So you can spend towards Etihad status. I like bonusing non-U.S. purchases, but if that’s meaningful to you then the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card is far better since it earns unlimited 3 points for every $1 spent on eligible foreign transactions. And I value Alaska’s miles far more than Etihad’s. But Etihad Gold Isn’t Qatar Gold When Qatar Airways launched its U.S. cards, the premium card’s first year of Gold status was immediately useful even to someone who never planned to fly Qatar. Qatar Gold is oneworld Sapphire. That means lounge access when flying American Airlines and Alaska Airlines, including domestic trips. It even gets you into American’s business class Flagship lounges on an eligible same-day itinerary. Etihad isn’t in an alliance. Their airline partnerships don’t turn Etihad Gold into an Admirals Club membership or give you those oneworld benefits on domestic American flights. The Premier card’s Priority Pass membership is a substantial nothingburger. Priority Pass is a drug on the market. Everyone offers Priority Pass. And Emirates gave its credit cards a purpose when it restricted first class awards to elite members. You need Silver status or higher to book a first class Classic Reward. You don’t need an Etihad card’s status just to redeem miles for the award you want. Etihad status can help when you actually fly Etihad, especially in coach. Lounge access and other benefits depend on your tier. But someone who mainly redeems miles for premium cabins already gets many of the things status would otherwise provide with their ticket. I’d Earn The Miles With A Different Card You don’t need an Etihad credit card to earn Etihad miles. Capital One, for instance, transfers to Etihad Guest at 1:1, and Venture and Venture X earn two miles per dollar on ordinary purchases. Citi and Bilt also offer transfers to Etihad. Put $40,000 of unbonused spend on the Etihad Premier card and earn 40,000 redeemable Etihad miles, while satisfying the spending requirement to keep Gold. Put that same spending on Venture X and earn 80,000 Capital One miles, which can become 80,000 Etihad miles. Or you can transfer them to a different airline. This is why I separate a card’s initial bonus and benefits from whether it’s worth using for spending. An Etihad bonus might help someone finish off an account for a specific award. That doesn’t make the card a good place to put their continuing spend. The narrow case I’d consider is someone who regularly buys Etihad coach tickets, will use the status benefits, and can retain Gold through $8,000 of Etihad purchases rather than diverting $40,000 of ordinary spending. For someone who wants Etihad miles for an occasional business or first class redemption, I’d earn transferable points with a better card. I wouldn’t pay $499 and give up half my everyday mileage earning just for Etihad Gold.     #168430. Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1470 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1470 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept.
    • The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.
    • According to recent reports, it's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From left, Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.

    According to recent reports, it's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States. Supporters overcame opposition from more than half the Democratic Caucus, which will be a factor when the bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess.

    The bill passed on a 62-33 vote, with 31 Democrats joining two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, in opposition.

    Shortly after the post-cloture time expired late Thursday, the Senate voted on passage of the legislation, including a substitute amendment consisting of revised text of the original permitting bill that the bipartisan authors unveiled before the midterm elections.

    However, the chamber did not consider any additional amendments to the bill, as initially planned by the sponsors, including Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., panel ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah, and panel ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

    The bill includes changes to how reviews are conducted and permits are issued under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Historic Preservation Act, Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act.

    It includes provisions intended to ensure electricity ratepayers are not saddled with the costs of bringing power to data centers, and would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission upcoming authority over interstate transmission lines.

    It also would provide legal recourse when administrations discriminate against certain forms of energy or seek to revisit permits on ideological grounds. That's intended in part to address the Trump administration’s actions to delay or block solar and wind energy projects.

    Democrats walked away from negotiations last year due to Trump administration actions to block offshore wind construction. However they ultimately said they received sufficient assurances that the administration would let stalled wind and solar projects move forward.

    The "major four" senators on the permitting bill solicited feedback and changes sought by various lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and were open to votes on additional amendments — so long as they didn't undo the measure's core tenets.

    "This bill has threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while, and we’ve got to take advantage of this opportunity," Capito remarked before passage.

    According to recent reports, ultimately, Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden would not consent to a time agreement allowing consideration of a finite number of amendments because Republicans wouldn't allow up-or-down votes at a simple-majority threshold on some of theirs. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to consider amendments on the floor.

    Wyden was pushing for a vote on an amendment that would prohibit construction of data centers on federal public lands. Merkley was pushing for amendments that included barring data centers from benefiting from “project certainty” protections against future presidents revoking their permits, and limiting presidential power to impose tariffs on clean energy project components, like wind turbines.

    The Senate had already adopted the substitute amendment introduced by the bill’s sponsors during a procedural vote on Wednesday. But the lack of a unanimous consent agreement to take up more amendments meant that an additional manager's package of changes to the substitute fell by the wayside.

    That amendment would have narrowed the instances where exemptions from National Historic Preservation Act reviews would be allowed, increased the annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund by 50 percent, and addressed concerns about the use of eminent domain when permitting transmission projects raised by Hawley and Rounds.

    The sponsors introduced an updated version of their manager’s amendment Thursday afternoon that would refine exemptions from the ratepayer projection provisions so that artificial intelligence "hyperscalers" can't escape through a loophole.

    The original manager's amendment sought to exempt internet and telecommunications providers' facilities, but the language was broad enough that cloud storage and other "information services" exclusions could potentially benefit data centers.

    None of those changes made it into the bill as a result of the stalemate over amendments, and Merkley objected on the floor to incorporating just the manager's package.

    According to recent reports, the bill has been endorsed by a wide range of industry groups, who argue that the current federal permitting regime makes it too difficult to finance, blueprint and construct projects domestically. This includes the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.

    The White House expressed its support for the bill in a statement of administration policy this month.

    The bill now moves on to the House, where it seemingly has the votes to pass.

    Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said last week that the bill can pass in that chamber, while a number of Democrats including the centrist Blue Dog Coalition and Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., co-chair of the bipartisan Climate Solutions Caucus, and Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., have expressed support.

    Budzinski was elected chair of the 112-member New Democrat Coalition last week for the next Congress, and that group issued a statement speaking favorably of permitting while stopping short of endorsing the bill as right now drafted.

    However, attendance on the House GOP side after Thanksgiving could be an issue: more than 30 lawmakers regularly skipped votes this week, the majority of them Republicans.

    And many Democrats have called on Heinrich and Whitehouse to punt consideration of the bill to the upcoming Congress, when their party will have large majorities in both chambers.

    According to recent reports, merkley, who is in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, and House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif. — the expected chairman of that panel — both said the bill included too many provisions Democrats opposed in order to garner Republican support.

    Some of the nation’s largest environmental groups including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council oppose the bill. A coalition of 17 Democratic states also expressed their opposition. And some Native American tribes and organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, also expressed their opposition.

    "I’m hoping to have a full opportunity to address the many legitimate concerns that stakeholders have raised with this bill," Merkley mentioned before the vote Thursday night.

    But Heinrich and Whitehouse resisted calls to delay the bill, arguing that President Donald Trump is in office for two more years and that any bill needs his support to be signed into law. They added that they will be able to address environmental complications under their majority, and that this bill would represent the “floor” of their ambitions.

    While Republicans have called for changes to the federal permitting system for decades, the effort gained steam with Democrats after the passage of their 2022 reconciliation law, which they dubbed the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

    As part of the deal to get then-Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Joe Manchin III, D-W.Va., on board with the IRA, the Biden administration agreed to support a bill overhauling the federal permitting system. Manchin introduced a bill that included changes to NEPA and transmission permitting, and would approve all remaining permits needed for the Mountain Valley Pipeline in his home state.

    However, his effort ultimately fell short on a 47-47 procedural vote to attach the bill to that year’s defense authorization measure.

    In the 118th Congress Manchin tried again, and in 2024 he and then-Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso, R-Wyo., introduced what Manchin called a “perfectly crafted balance.” The committee approved that bill in July 2024, but it was never voted on by the full Senate.

    Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich made a collective commitment to address permitting overhaul when they stepped into their current roles in January 2025, and spent nearly 21 months working on the legislation.

    Since Manchin’s first bill, the political calculus changed.

    Industry observers note that after decades of stagnant energy demand, electricity prices began rising in part due to the expansion of data centers. Consumers also became increasingly frustrated with their local utilities over affordability concerns, which in turn spurred more lawmakers across the country, including on Capitol Hill, to critically examine their practices.

    Lee also pushed for language streamlining NHPA reviews, which had not been a focus of earlier permitting discussion. He's argued that the law has expanded beyond its originally intended scope and become a major barrier to infrastructure projects in Western states like Utah.

    Breaking: Delta Plans Seattle To Singapore A350 Flights, Carrier’s Third Longest Route

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia.
    • Sources indicate that A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed intends to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan.
    • As Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia. It’s an area where Delta has increasingly fallen behind United in recent years, but Delta now hopes to not only catch up, but even beat United. We’ll see what comes of that, and in particular, find out just how costly that growth is.

    Sources indicate that A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed intends to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan. Executives also confirmed out of which airport the service would operate. There’s now an additional enhancement, as an announcement about the fresh route is imminent, which almost certainly points to a fall 2027 launch for the service.

    As Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. So, what kind of expansion should we expect?

    Back in August 2026, Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito explicitly confirmed that the airline would return to Singapore. What was perhaps most interesting is that he also indirectly confirmed the hub out of which the service would operate — Esposito ruled out that the service could operate out of Los Angeles, so it’s pretty clear that the airline will operate this service out of Seattle (SEA).

    That’s also what JonNYC reported in the past, and now we can take that a step further — Delta is holding an event in Seattle in early December 2026, and that’s when the airline is expected to announce the service.

    My guess is that we’re looking at a fall 2027 service start, at best. At 8,070 miles, this will be Delta’s third longest flight, after its routes to South Africa, which are from Atlanta (ATL) to Cape Town (CPT) and Johannesburg (JNB).

    One certainly wonders if this Singapore route could be operated by Delta’s newly introduced Airbus A350-1000s, which will feature an all-new passenger experience. While the plane has great range and per seat economics, the only thing I’d say is that it’s “a lot of plane” for a new market, in terms of the overall capacity (even with the very premium layout).

    Industry observers note that in both the Seattle and Los Angeles to Singapore market, Singapore Airlines is the only other carrier operating. So competitively there’s not a huge difference in that regard, though Los Angeles is a significantly larger market in terms of demand for Singapore, and for that matter, Singapore Airlines also has more service out of the airport. But perhaps Delta is also looking to beat Alaska to the punch in the Seattle market.

    It’s fantastic to see Delta looking to grow its presence in Asia. Point-to-point flying to Asia is a market that United has basically had cornered in recent years, and competition is good for consumers.

    It has been revealed that it’s amazing to think for how many years Delta basically squandered its Asia advantage. Keep in mind that back in the day, Northwest had a robust Asia network, and after the merger with Delta, we saw that network decreased slowly but steadily, as Delta instead focused on routing everything through Seoul Incheon, and into the Korean Air network. So I’m happy to see a reversal of that strategy.

    I also have to say that given Delta’s hubris, it’s kind of fun to see the airline having to increasingly play “catch up,” rather than coming in as the dominant carrier. And I think that very much sums up what’s going on in Asia.

    Sources indicate that the most basic structural disadvantage that Delta has is that United has a fortress hub in San Francisco (SFO), which is where a large part of its Asia network flies from. That’s fantastic for connectivity, not to mention San Francisco is a very strong market for Asia traffic.

    Recent findings suggest that delta, meanwhile, is taking a split hub approach, flying out of both Los Angeles and Seattle. Obviously Delta is trying to make the best of its situation, but there’s no denying that this is an uphill battle:.

    It also has to be emphasized that in terms of actually transporting passengers profitably (or at less of a loss), United does a better job at that than Delta, despite its lower overall profitability. Comparing passenger revenue per air seat mile to cost per air seat mile, United is at 16.18 cents vs. 16.46 cents, while Delta is at 17.37 cents vs. 19.31 cents.

    Delta is growing quite a bit in Asia at the moment. The airline has already launched flights to Hong Kong, with flights now on sale to Manila and Tokyo Narita. On top of that, Delta is expected to announce a fresh Seattle to Singapore route within the next two weeks, with a launch likely planned for the fall of 2027.

    It’s great for passengers to see more competition across the Pacific, as Delta sure is making up for a lack of effort for years. However, the airline will also have quite the disadvantage compared to United for a long time….

    What do you make of Delta’s aims to fly to Singapore?

    Citi AAdvantage Executive Card Review: Better Lounges And More Status Credit

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 55 min read (11084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
    • Recent findings suggest that the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] costs $695 a year, but I think it’s a better value today than it was at $595.
    • Recent findings suggest that I have the card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

    Recent findings suggest that the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] costs $695 a year, but I think it’s a better value today than it was at $595. American Airlines is investing seriously in its clubs again, and the card’s refresh added more credit towards elite status and benefits I can actually use.

    Recent findings suggest that I have the card. For a regular American Airlines flyer who wants Admirals Club access, it’s the place to start. The lounges are getting better, more are coming, and buying membership directly from American costs hundreds of dollars more.

    Sources indicate that when I covered the refresh, I thought the additional Loyalty Points alone justified the $100 annual fee increase for me. Citi has since added $200 in annual inKind dining credits, too.

    The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® includes full Admirals Club membership for the primary cardmember. American has priced standalone membership to make getting the card the obvious choice for someone eligible to apply. Here’s the current comparison: Option   Annual Cost   What You Get Citi AAdvantage Executive card   $695   Full membership, including guest privileges and eligible partner lounges Full membership bought from American   $1,200–$1,400, depending on status   Full membership, including guest privileges and eligible partner lounges Single membership bought from American   $750   Admirals Club access for the member, without guests or partner lounges Even an Executive Platinum member pays $1,200 for full membership. The card saves $505 before assigning any value to its miles, status bonuses or credits. Someone without status saves $705. And the card costs less than American’s restricted $750 membership option. There’s no annual visit allowance to ration and no spending requirement to unlock unlimited visits. Qualifying Citigold customers can receive a $145 annual relationship credit, reducing their cost further. What The Lounge Access Includes American has nearly 50 Admirals Clubs, with more than 60 partner lounges extending the membership’s reach. Under American’s access rules: You can visit Admirals Clubs on eligible same-day itineraries, including American Airlines and oneworld flights. You don’t have to buy the ticket with this card. You can bring two guests or your immediate family—a spouse or domestic partner and children under 18. Guests need eligible same-day boarding passes, too. The primary cardmember’s membership includes eligible partner locations, such as Alaska Lounges and Qantas Clubs. The flight requirements vary by partner. This doesn’t include Flagship Lounges or Flagship Dining. Executive Platinum status by itself doesn’t get you into Admirals Clubs on ordinary domestic trips. Neither does a typical domestic first class ticket. The card also has an unusually good deal for additional cardholders: $175 total for up to three authorized consumers, then $175 for each additional user. Use all three slots and that’s about $58 per person annually. Each authorized user can visit Admirals Clubs without you and bring their own eligible guests. They need their physical card, identification and an eligible same-day boarding pass. They get Admirals Club access, rather than full membership, so they don’t get the partner lounge benefit. For a family, $870 in total annual fees can cover a primary cardmember and three authorized users traveling separately, with guest privileges. That’s less than American charges one Executive Platinum member for standalone full membership. If you only want a few visits a year, the $350 annual fee Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] includes four annual Admirals Club passes. American Is Finally Building Clubs I Want To Spend Time In For years American underinvested in lounges. They closed clubs, and when they renovated others the result was often the institutional look I’ve called “modern hospital.” The newer design is a huge improvement. Washington National’s E concourse club, Denver, Newark and Philadelphia show where American is going: warmer wood, better lighting, comfortable seating and spaces that feel inviting. I like this aesthetic more than the newer United Clubs or Delta Sky Clubs. The food has improved, too. I still generally prefer Delta’s lounge food, but American has moved well beyond the old snacks-and-soup proposition. Their fall Admirals Club menus include beef barbacoa taco bars in Chicago, Denver and St. Louis; sesame orange chicken at several West Coast clubs and Phoenix; and Creole style chicken with white bean cassoulet at the Fresh York and Newark clubs. I’ve covered American’s plan for a new, renovated or expanded lounge nearly every month, on average, over two to three years. That’s very different from what we saw for much of the past decade. Among the projects: Charlotte: A new Admirals Club exceeding 40,000 square feet, with showers and multiple bars and food stations. Dallas–Fort Worth: A 37,000 square foot Terminal C club, plus a Provisions location planned for Terminal F. Austin: A replacement club exceeding 12,000 square feet, with American’s first outdoor lounge terrace. Chicago, Nashville, Miami and Washington National: New or expanded clubs, including Chicago’s L concourse project and the refresh of National’s Concourse D club. There’s also the Provisions grab-and-go concept, already operating in Charlotte, with additional locations announced for New York JFK and Dallas–Fort Worth. Sometimes you want food to take to the gate more than you want a seat in a lounge. And the most valuable part of a club can still be its agents. I’ve written about the Austin agents who keep looking for better connections after I’ve left. Having someone help fix a disrupted trip can be worth more than everything you eat and drink in the lounge that year. The Initial Bonus And Who Can Get It The current public initial bonus is 80,000 AAdvantage miles after $8,000 in purchases within the first three months of account opening. The annual fee is $695. Those are redeemable miles. The initial bonus doesn’t count as Loyalty Points towards status, although eligible spending to earn it does. Under Citi’s terms, you aren’t eligible for the initial bonus if you’ve received an Executive card new account bonus within the past 48 months. The restriction also covers converting another Citi card into an Executive account when that other account earned a new account bonus within the last 48 months. Simply having a different AAdvantage cobrand card doesn’t disqualify you. Up To 40,000 Extra Loyalty Points Without Spending On The Card The card awards 10,000 additional Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds during the AAdvantage qualification year, which runs March through February: Account Reaches   Cumulative Executive Card Bonuses 50,000 Loyalty Points   10,000 Loyalty Points 90,000 Loyalty Points   20,000 Loyalty Points 165,000 Loyalty Points   30,000 Loyalty Points 240,000 Loyalty Points   40,000 Loyalty Points The last two bonuses were added in the refresh. You don’t have to earn the qualifying Loyalty Points by spending on this card. Flying, shopping portal earnings, hotel bookings and spending on other AAdvantage cards can get you there. The bonuses themselves count towards subsequent thresholds. Earn 80,000 Loyalty Points outside this benefit and the first two bonuses bring you to 100,000. For someone pursuing Executive Platinum, the card can supply 30,000 of the required 200,000 Loyalty Points. Earning 170,000 elsewhere gets you there. The fourth bonus comes after Executive Platinum, helping towards higher Loyalty Point Rewards: 210,000 earned elsewhere plus the four bonuses gets you to 250,000. This is why the Executive card can make sense alongside another AAdvantage card. I have the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], too, and its spending can help trigger these Executive card bonuses. Globe’s Flight Streak bonuses can also stack with them. The Credits That Help Pay For The Card The October inKind addition is especially useful to me. I already use inKind at restaurants I’d eat at anyway. Here’s how the recurring credits work: $200 inKind dining credit: $100 for January–June and $100 for July–December. Add the card and benefit in the inKind app, then apply the credit when paying a participating restaurant through the app. There’s no minimum spend, and you can use it across multiple checks. Unused credit doesn’t carry over. Tips aren’t covered, and authorized users share the account’s allocation. Up to $500 American Airlines Vacations credit: Up to $250 in each half of the calendar year. This covers eligible vacation packages and Experiences purchased through American Airlines Vacations. Packages require at least two travel components, such as a flight and hotel or flight and car. Up to $100 for inflight and eligible Admirals Club purchases: A calendar year statement credit for eligible purchases charged to the card. Club food and beverages qualify. The inflight benefit applies to eligible domestic American Airlines and American Eagle flights. I won’t value this at the full $100 because many of the drinks and snacks I’d otherwise buy are already included through my status or seat, but it can cover additional purchases for family or premium club drinks. Up to $120 for Avis and Budget: Each calendar year, for eligible prepaid rentals booked directly at avis.com or budget.com and charged to the card. Pay later reservations and bookings through other travel sites don’t qualify. Up to $180 in Lyft credits: Take three eligible rides paid with the card in a calendar month, then receive a $15 Lyft credit. The credit expires after 30 days. This improved from $10 to $15 per month, but three rides are still required. Starting February 1, 2027, Wait & Save rides won’t qualify. If inKind saves you $200 on dining you’d otherwise pay for, that leaves $495 of annual fee to justify with lounge access, status bonuses and the other benefits. One old benefit is being phased out: the $10 Grubhub credit per monthly billing statement. Accounts opened before August 23, 2026 retain it through August 31, 2027. New applicants don’t get it, and the old 25% inflight food and beverage rebate has ended (replaced by the annual $100 credit). Hotel, Rental Car And Airport Benefits The refresh also added Omni Champion status and the ability to earn an annual free night. Enroll in the status benefit before your stay, allowing up to 14 days for activation. Then complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights, booked directly with Omni in your name and paid with the Executive card. That earns 100 Omni Credits for a free night on a later stay, once per calendar year. Redeem within 12 months. Taxes and resort fees are included in the award. A two-night stay you were going to make anyway can produce a valuable additional night. You can also enroll in Avis President’s Club through August 31, 2028. This offers upgrades and other rental benefits, although it’s duplicative for members who already receive it by reaching 100,000 AAdvantage Loyalty Points. Other benefits include: First checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for the tickets with the card. Priority check-in, priority security where available and Group 4 boarding for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. Up to $120 towards Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years when you pay the application fee with the card. No foreign transaction fees and travel protections including trip cancellation and interruption, trip delay, lost baggage and rental car coverage for qualifying purchases. What I’d Actually Spend On The Card The earning rates are: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings. 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases. 1 mile per dollar on other eligible purchases. Eligible spending earns one Loyalty Point per dollar. The category bonuses don’t multiply that: a dollar of American Airlines spending earns four redeemable miles and one Loyalty Point from the card. AAdvantage Hotels can separately award miles and Loyalty Points for the booking itself. The 12-mile rate is a strong reason to use this card when booking through American’s hotel and rental car platforms. I’d also use it where payment is required to earn a credit or benefit. For everyday spending, the decision is how much the additional Loyalty Points help you. American lets card spending make a real contribution to status, but earning one redeemable mile per dollar means giving up the rewards another card would have earned. You can keep the Executive card for its clubs and milestone bonuses while putting spending on a different card. After $150,000 in purchases during a calendar year, eligible American Airlines purchases earn five miles per dollar for the rest of that year. I wouldn’t do that just to earn one additional mile per dollar on subsequent airfare.     It has been revealed that the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® includes full Admirals Club membership for the primary cardmember. American has priced standalone membership to make getting the card the obvious choice for someone eligible to apply.

    In a recent development, even an Executive Platinum member pays $1,200 for full membership. The card saves $505 before assigning any value to its miles, status bonuses or credits. Someone without status saves $705. And the card costs less than American’s restricted $750 membership option. There’s no annual visit allowance to ration and no spending requirement to unlock unlimited visits. Qualifying Citigold customers can receive a $145 annual relationship credit, reducing their cost further.

    American has nearly 50 Admirals Clubs, with more than 60 partner lounges extending the membership’s reach. Under American’s access rules: You can visit Admirals Clubs on eligible same-day itineraries, including American Airlines and oneworld flights. You don’t have to buy the ticket with this card. You can bring two guests or your immediate family—a spouse or domestic partner and children under 18. Guests need eligible same-day boarding passes, too. The primary cardmember’s membership includes eligible partner locations, such as Alaska Lounges and Qantas Clubs. The flight requirements vary by partner. This doesn’t include Flagship Lounges or Flagship Dining. Executive Platinum status by itself doesn’t get you into Admirals Clubs on ordinary domestic trips. Neither does a typical domestic first class ticket. The card also has an unusually good deal for additional cardholders: $175 total for up to three authorized consumers, then $175 for each additional user. Use all three slots and that’s about $58 per person annually. Each authorized user can visit Admirals Clubs without you and bring their own eligible guests. They need their physical card, identification and an eligible same-day boarding pass. They get Admirals Club access, rather than full membership, so they don’t get the partner lounge benefit. For a family, $870 in total annual fees can cover a primary cardmember and three authorized users traveling separately, with guest privileges. That’s less than American charges one Executive Platinum member for standalone full membership. If you only want a few visits a year, the $350 annual fee Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] includes four annual Admirals Club passes. American Is Finally Building Clubs I Want To Spend Time In For years American underinvested in lounges. They closed clubs, and when they renovated others the result was often the institutional look I’ve called “modern hospital.” The newer design is a huge improvement. Washington National’s E concourse club, Denver, Newark and Philadelphia show where American is going: warmer wood, better lighting, comfortable seating and spaces that feel inviting. I like this aesthetic more than the newer United Clubs or Delta Sky Clubs. The food has improved, too. I still generally prefer Delta’s lounge food, but American has moved well beyond the old snacks-and-soup proposition. Their fall Admirals Club menus include beef barbacoa taco bars in Chicago, Denver and St. Louis; sesame orange chicken at several West Coast clubs and Phoenix; and Creole style chicken with white bean cassoulet at the Fresh York and Newark clubs. I’ve covered American’s proposal for a new, renovated or expanded lounge nearly every month, on average, over two to three years. That’s very different from what we saw for much of the past decade. Among the projects: Charlotte: A new Admirals Club exceeding 40,000 square feet, with showers and multiple bars and food stations. Dallas–Fort Worth: A 37,000 square foot Terminal C club, plus a Provisions location planned for Terminal F. Austin: A replacement club exceeding 12,000 square feet, with American’s first outdoor lounge terrace. Chicago, Nashville, Miami and Washington National: New or expanded clubs, including Chicago’s L concourse project and the refresh of National’s Concourse D club. There’s also the Provisions grab-and-go concept, already operating in Charlotte, with additional locations revealed for New York JFK and Dallas–Fort Worth. Sometimes you want food to take to the gate more than you want a seat in a lounge. And the most valuable part of a club can still be its agents. I’ve written about the Austin agents who keep looking for better connections after I’ve left. Having someone help fix a disrupted trip can be worth more than everything you eat and drink in the lounge that year. The Initial Bonus And Who Can Get It The current public initial bonus is 80,000 AAdvantage miles after $8,000 in purchases within the first three months of account opening. The annual fee is $695. Those are redeemable miles. The initial bonus doesn’t count as Loyalty Points towards status, although eligible spending to earn it does. Under Citi’s terms, you aren’t eligible for the initial bonus if you’ve received an Executive card new account bonus within the past 48 months. The restriction also covers converting another Citi card into an Executive account when that other account earned a new account bonus within the last 48 months. Simply having a different AAdvantage cobrand card doesn’t disqualify you. Up To 40,000 Extra Loyalty Points Without Spending On The Card The card awards 10,000 additional Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds during the AAdvantage qualification year, which runs March through February: Account Reaches   Cumulative Executive Card Bonuses 50,000 Loyalty Points   10,000 Loyalty Points 90,000 Loyalty Points   20,000 Loyalty Points 165,000 Loyalty Points   30,000 Loyalty Points 240,000 Loyalty Points   40,000 Loyalty Points The last two bonuses were added in the refresh. You don’t have to earn the qualifying Loyalty Points by spending on this card. Flying, shopping portal earnings, hotel bookings and spending on other AAdvantage cards can get you there. The bonuses themselves count towards subsequent thresholds. Earn 80,000 Loyalty Points outside this benefit and the first two bonuses bring you to 100,000. For someone pursuing Executive Platinum, the card can supply 30,000 of the required 200,000 Loyalty Points. Earning 170,000 elsewhere gets you there. The fourth bonus comes after Executive Platinum, helping towards higher Loyalty Point Rewards: 210,000 earned elsewhere plus the four bonuses gets you to 250,000. This is why the Executive card can make sense alongside another AAdvantage card. I have the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], too, and its spending can help trigger these Executive card bonuses. Globe’s Flight Streak bonuses can also stack with them. The Credits That Help Pay For The Card The October inKind addition is especially useful to me. I already use inKind at restaurants I’d eat at anyway. Here’s how the recurring credits work: $200 inKind dining credit: $100 for January–June and $100 for July–December. Add the card and benefit in the inKind app, then apply the credit when paying a participating restaurant through the app. There’s no minimum spend, and you can use it across multiple checks. Unused credit doesn’t carry over. Tips aren’t covered, and authorized users share the account’s allocation. Up to $500 American Airlines Vacations credit: Up to $250 in each half of the calendar year. This covers eligible vacation packages and Experiences purchased through American Airlines Vacations. Packages require at least two travel components, such as a flight and hotel or flight and car. Up to $100 for inflight and eligible Admirals Club purchases: A calendar year statement credit for eligible purchases charged to the card. Club food and beverages qualify. The inflight benefit applies to eligible domestic American Airlines and American Eagle flights. I won’t value this at the full $100 because many of the drinks and snacks I’d otherwise buy are already included through my status or seat, but it can cover additional purchases for family or premium club drinks. Up to $120 for Avis and Budget: Each calendar year, for eligible prepaid rentals booked directly at avis.com or budget.com and charged to the card. Pay later reservations and bookings through other travel sites don’t qualify. Up to $180 in Lyft credits: Take three eligible rides paid with the card in a calendar month, then receive a $15 Lyft credit. The credit expires after 30 days. This improved from $10 to $15 per month, but three rides are still required. Starting February 1, 2027, Wait & Save rides won’t qualify. If inKind saves you $200 on dining you’d otherwise pay for, that leaves $495 of annual fee to justify with lounge access, status bonuses and the other benefits. One old benefit is being phased out: the $10 Grubhub credit per monthly billing statement. Accounts opened before August 23, 2026 retain it through August 31, 2027. New applicants don’t get it, and the old 25% inflight food and beverage rebate has ended (replaced by the annual $100 credit). Hotel, Rental Car And Airport Benefits The refresh also added Omni Champion status and the ability to earn an annual free night. Enroll in the status benefit before your stay, allowing up to 14 days for activation. Then complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights, booked directly with Omni in your name and paid with the Executive card. That earns 100 Omni Credits for a free night on a later stay, once per calendar year. Redeem within 12 months. Taxes and resort fees are included in the award. A two-night stay you were going to make anyway can produce a valuable additional night. You can also enroll in Avis President’s Club through August 31, 2028. This offers upgrades and other rental benefits, although it’s duplicative for members who already receive it by reaching 100,000 AAdvantage Loyalty Points. Other benefits include: First checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for the tickets with the card. Priority check-in, priority security where available and Group 4 boarding for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. Up to $120 towards Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years when you pay the application fee with the card. No foreign transaction fees and travel protections including trip cancellation and interruption, trip delay, lost baggage and rental car coverage for qualifying purchases. What I’d Actually Spend On The Card The earning rates are: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings. 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases. 1 mile per dollar on other eligible purchases. Eligible spending earns one Loyalty Point per dollar. The category bonuses don’t multiply that: a dollar of American Airlines spending earns four redeemable miles and one Loyalty Point from the card. AAdvantage Hotels can separately award miles and Loyalty Points for the booking itself. The 12-mile rate is a strong reason to use this card when booking through American’s hotel and rental car platforms. I’d also use it where payment is required to earn a credit or benefit. For everyday spending, the decision is how much the additional Loyalty Points help you. American lets card spending make a real contribution to status, but earning one redeemable mile per dollar means giving up the rewards another card would have earned. You can keep the Executive card for its clubs and milestone bonuses while putting spending on a different card. After $150,000 in purchases during a calendar year, eligible American Airlines purchases earn five miles per dollar for the rest of that year. I wouldn’t do that just to earn one additional mile per dollar on subsequent airfare.     It has been revealed that the card awards 10,000 additional Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds during the AAdvantage qualification year, which runs March through February: Account Reaches   Cumulative Executive Card Bonuses 50,000 Loyalty Points   10,000 Loyalty Points 90,000 Loyalty Points   20,000 Loyalty Points 165,000 Loyalty Points   30,000 Loyalty Points 240,000 Loyalty Points   40,000 Loyalty Points The last two bonuses were added in the refresh. You don’t have to earn the qualifying Loyalty Points by spending on this card. Flying, shopping portal earnings, hotel bookings and spending on other AAdvantage cards can get you there. The bonuses themselves count towards subsequent thresholds. Earn 80,000 Loyalty Points outside this benefit and the first two bonuses bring you to 100,000. For someone pursuing Executive Platinum, the card can supply 30,000 of the required 200,000 Loyalty Points. Earning 170,000 elsewhere gets you there. The fourth bonus comes after Executive Platinum, helping towards higher Loyalty Point Rewards: 210,000 earned elsewhere plus the four bonuses gets you to 250,000. This is why the Executive card can make sense alongside another AAdvantage card. I have the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], too, and its spending can help trigger these Executive card bonuses. Globe’s Flight Streak bonuses can also stack with them. The Credits That Help Pay For The Card The October inKind addition is especially useful to me. I already use inKind at restaurants I’d eat at anyway. Here’s how the recurring credits work: $200 inKind dining credit: $100 for January–June and $100 for July–December. Add the card and benefit in the inKind app, then apply the credit when paying a participating restaurant through the app. There’s no minimum spend, and you can use it across multiple checks. Unused credit doesn’t carry over. Tips aren’t covered, and authorized users share the account’s allocation. Up to $500 American Airlines Vacations credit: Up to $250 in each half of the calendar year. This covers eligible vacation packages and Experiences purchased through American Airlines Vacations. Packages require at least two travel components, such as a flight and hotel or flight and car. Up to $100 for inflight and eligible Admirals Club purchases: A calendar year statement credit for eligible purchases charged to the card. Club food and beverages qualify. The inflight benefit applies to eligible domestic American Airlines and American Eagle flights. I won’t value this at the full $100 because many of the drinks and snacks I’d otherwise buy are already included through my status or seat, but it can cover additional purchases for family or premium club drinks. Up to $120 for Avis and Budget: Each calendar year, for eligible prepaid rentals booked directly at avis.com or budget.com and charged to the card. Pay later reservations and bookings through other travel sites don’t qualify. Up to $180 in Lyft credits: Take three eligible rides paid with the card in a calendar month, then receive a $15 Lyft credit. The credit expires after 30 days. This improved from $10 to $15 per month, but three rides are still required. Starting February 1, 2027, Wait & Save rides won’t qualify. If inKind saves you $200 on dining you’d otherwise pay for, that leaves $495 of annual fee to justify with lounge access, status bonuses and the other benefits. One old benefit is being phased out: the $10 Grubhub credit per monthly billing statement. Accounts opened before August 23, 2026 retain it through August 31, 2027. Fresh applicants don’t get it, and the old 25% inflight food and beverage rebate has ended (replaced by the annual $100 credit). Hotel, Rental Car And Airport Benefits The refresh also added Omni Champion status and the ability to earn an annual free night. Enroll in the status benefit before your stay, allowing up to 14 days for activation. Then complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights, booked directly with Omni in your name and paid with the Executive card. That earns 100 Omni Credits for a free night on a later stay, once per calendar year. Redeem within 12 months. Taxes and resort fees are included in the award. A two-night stay you were going to make anyway can produce a valuable additional night. You can also enroll in Avis President’s Club through August 31, 2028. This offers upgrades and other rental benefits, although it’s duplicative for members who already receive it by reaching 100,000 AAdvantage Loyalty Points. Other benefits include: First checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for the tickets with the card. Priority check-in, priority security where available and Group 4 boarding for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. Up to $120 towards Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years when you pay the application fee with the card. No foreign transaction fees and travel protections including trip cancellation and interruption, trip delay, lost baggage and rental car coverage for qualifying purchases. What I’d Actually Spend On The Card The earning rates are: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings. 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases. 1 mile per dollar on other eligible purchases. Eligible spending earns one Loyalty Point per dollar. The category bonuses don’t multiply that: a dollar of American Airlines spending earns four redeemable miles and one Loyalty Point from the card. AAdvantage Hotels can separately award miles and Loyalty Points for the booking itself. The 12-mile rate is a strong reason to use this card when booking through American’s hotel and rental car platforms. I’d also use it where payment is required to earn a credit or benefit. For everyday spending, the decision is how much the additional Loyalty Points help you. American lets card spending make a real contribution to status, but earning one redeemable mile per dollar means giving up the rewards another card would have earned. You can keep the Executive card for its clubs and milestone bonuses while putting spending on a different card. After $150,000 in purchases during a calendar year, eligible American Airlines purchases earn five miles per dollar for the rest of that year. I wouldn’t do that just to earn one additional mile per dollar on subsequent airfare.     Industry News: Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Points With 80% Bonus (1.1 Cents Each): Worth It?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is right now offering a best-ever promotion on purchased points.
    • Link: Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points with a bonus.
    • Industry observers note that between 12AM GMT on November 24 and 11:59PM GMT on December 31, 2026, the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club program is offering a bonus on purchased points.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is right now offering a best-ever promotion on purchased points. Through December 31, 2026, Flying Club members can purchase points with up to an 80% bonus, which is potentially an opportunity to buy points for under 1.1 cents each. Suffice it to say that this could be a very attractive deal.

    Link: Buy Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points with a bonus.

    Industry observers note that between 12AM GMT on November 24 and 11:59PM GMT on December 31, 2026, the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club program is offering a bonus on purchased points. Virgin Atlantic is offering a tiered bonus of up to 80%, as follows:.

    Note that the purchase of Virgin Atlantic points is non-refundable, and purchasing points doesn’t count toward Flying Club elite status. Points will be credited to accounts within 24 hours, though they typically post faster than that, and almost instantly.

    The cost to purchase Virgin Atlantic points varies based on where your account is registered:.

    Sources indicate that the pricing is much better for those with accounts registered in the UK rather than the US. Assuming you’re eligible for an 80% bonus:.

    So as you can see, in the United States you can potentially pay 1.39 cents per point, while in the UK you can potentially pay 1.09 cents per point.

    It’s interesting how much Virgin Atlantic penalizes those in the United States when it comes to buying points. Then again, when it comes to overall points earning opportunities, we can’t really complain in the United States, given the amazing credit card offers we have.

    Sources indicate that virgin Atlantic Flying Club ordinarily lets members purchase up to 200,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been doubled, to 400,000 points.

    In a recent development, when Virgin Atlantic Flying Club offers a promotion on purchased points, the best version of the offer is almost always for a 70% bonus. As you can tell, this offer is even better than those, as this is truly a best-ever offer. Personally, I’d recommend buying points based on when you have a short term use in mind, rather than based on the slight difference in the cost per point.

    Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the Flying Club program, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

    Recent findings suggest that flying Club points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

    According to recent reports, virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

    Nowadays Virgin Atlantic has dynamic award pricing for its own flights, and for those with flexibility who want the best deal, this can make for some great deals. For example, there are some transatlantic one-way business class awards that cost under 30,000 points, which is amazing.

    Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

    Paying 52,500-60,000 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with.

    All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

    Industry observers note that everyone will value points currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Flying Club points to be worth 1.1 cents each. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from Flying Club points than that.

    It has been revealed that virgin Atlantic Flying Club points don’t expire. There’s no requirement to even have any account activity, as the points will never expire regardless.

    While buying Virgin Atlantic points could represent a great deal, keep in mind that there are lots of other ways to earn Flying Club points. Most significantly, Virgin Atlantic is partners with major transferable points currencies, including American Express Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, and Citi ThankYou, and in all cases, points can be moved at a 1:1 ratio. There are several ways to earn these points aside from outright buying them.

    Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is offering members an 80% bonus on purchased points, which is an opportunity to buy points for 1.09-1.39 cents each (in USD), depending on where your account is registered.

    There are plenty of circumstances where this could be a great deal. The only major consideration is that there are lots of other ways to earn Virgin Atlantic points with transferable points currencies, so some may prefer to earn rewards that way. With a specific use in mind, there could definitely be huge value in buying Flying Club points.

    Do you initiative on buying Virgin Atlantic Flying Club points with a bonus?

    Sources indicate that membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

    The recent Saturday Night Live “Sister” skit hit a nerve with its fake ad for a 24-hour elder-care service. The service is “completely free,” provided you’re the brother.

    “My dad means the world to me,” it begins, with comedian John Mulaney narrating. “So, when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible. I didn’t want to put him in a nursing home, but a private health aide could cost thousands a week. I didn’t know where to turn.”.

    Latest Update: Spirit Airlines Shut Down—Did It Forget To Cancel Its Internet? Comcast Wants $1.25 Million

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Spirit Airlines stopped flying in May, but Comcast and its subsidiaries say it still owes $1.25 million in internet bills.
    • Sources indicate that part of this sounds like Spirit forgot to turn off its internet when it moved out.
    • Recent findings suggest that their November 19 court filing asks the bankruptcy judge to order payment and make Spirit decide whether to keep or reject the contracts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Spirit Airlines stopped flying in May, but Comcast and its subsidiaries say it still owes $1.25 million in internet bills. Some charges are for locations Spirit indicates it left in 2024—but the providers say they haven’t produced records showing the service was canceled. Always keep proof when dealing with Comcast! Part of this sounds like Spirit forgot to turn off its internet when it moved out. According to the providers, on October 22 the airline authorized them to disconnect every location except Dania Pointe in Dania Beach, Florida. That was nearly six months after the airline stopped flying. Their November 19 court filing asks the bankruptcy judge to order payment and make Spirit decide whether to keep or reject the contracts. Comcast and its Masergy subsidiary say some services were still running when they filed. Spirit shut down on May 2 after it couldn’t obtain the money to keep operating. No one would continue to fund its massive losses. But the bankruptcy process to unwind its business remains ongoing. There are assets to sell, contracts to resolve, records to maintain and creditors arguing over who gets paid. I’ve covered the lawsuit from workers seeking 60 days of pay over the abrupt shutdown and the court-approved $668 million sale of a 27-aircraft portfolio. Much of that aircraft price represented lenders applying what Spirit owed them toward their purchase. The four internet providers list these unpaid balances: Provider Amount Claimed Comcast Cable Communications Management $219,743.41 Masergy Cloud Communications $164,626.99 Masergy Communications $849,646.45 Nitel $11,990.73 Total $1,246,007.58 Comcast acquired Masergy in 2021 and Nitel in 2025. This is for internet service at Spirit locations, not inflight wifi (which was provided by Thales). The providers say they’ve repeatedly sought payment. Spirit responded that some locations had been vacated in 2024, and that disconnection requests should have been submitted for others. You might expect the internet companies simply to get in line with Spirit’s other unpaid creditors. For bills dating to before the bankruptcy, that’s probably what happens. But these companies say they continued providing services after Spirit filed on August 29, 2025. Necessary expenses of running a firm in bankruptcy can qualify as administrative expenses, which get priority over other unsecured debts, or else no one would keep supplying a bankrupt business trying to turn itself around. And services needed to sell its assets and administer the remaining business can continue to qualify. It’s unclear what treatment will apply to internet Spirit was no longer using, even if it hadn’t cancelled the contracts. Comcast needs to establish the benefit their services supplied to the bankruptcy estate. In fact, their motion cites In re Enron but that denied administrative priority for unused pipeline capacity that hadn’t benefited the estate. Internet connections supporting the Spirit Airlines liquidation are likely to get repayment priority But defunct services that hadn’t merely been cancelled might not. A hearing is scheduled for December 16, with responses due December 9. And even a successful priority claim doesn’t necessarily mean Comcast gets immediate payment. In Midway Airlines, a telephone equipment lessor won an administrative claim for unpaid lease obligations, but the appeals court upheld making it wait for payment alongside other administrative creditors. So Comcast may have to wait as long for payment as you wait on hold to schedule a service appointment. Topics on this pageBankruptcyComcastSpirit AirlinesFlorida+1 more More From View from the Wing.

    Breaking: Island Mayor Pleads With Japan Airlines Mileage Runners After Locals Can’t Book Flights

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way.
    • News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused concerns for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.
    • According to recent reports, while the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

    News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused concerns for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

    According to recent reports, while the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

    According to recent reports, this ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

    Recent findings suggest that at Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:.

    According to recent reports, the issue is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:.

    Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”.

    Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

    I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

    Sources indicate that while it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

    While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a fresh restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

    Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

    Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

    Ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the problem here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

    What do you make of this Japan Airlines mileage run promotion situation?

    Your feedback is important in helping us keep our community safe.

    In a recent development, JAL has some tools they could use. One would be to hike prices with a "locals discount" or to limit cheap fares in other ways. Another would be to just comp the miles for existing tickets. But part of the glitch is probably the lifetime status program that JAL has. Five points per domestic leg times 12 equals 60 points per day. With lifetime status at 1500 points conveying OWS (and with it, you know, lifetime lounge access)...honestly, the prospect of blowing a few weeks flying around in Okinawa isn't utterly irrational.

    Perhaps not the best analogue given the difference in the size and scale, but the main domestic airlines in Taiwan, Mandarin Airlines (China Airlines) and Uni Air (EVA Air) have long made their domestic routes to remote islands ineligible for mileage earnings. Perhaps JAL needs to consider something similar….

    Sources indicate that the story is actually from February 2026. JAL corrected it for next years promo with a bonus limit.

    Just modify the promo to exclude short flights - say less than 500 miles. Or limit the number of flights per day with the promo - say 2.

    "Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community..." The mayor should have called on JAL to consider its impact, not just the milage runners.
