    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk.
    • Recent findings suggest that we finally woke up and shook it off.
    • It has been revealed that the historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, America has been in a funk. The whole country has seemed to be in a sour mood, unhappy with everything, feeling as if the world has gone off its axis and life is out of balance. The trauma of that experience was probably far deeper and more injurious than we wanted to admit, so we just sort of sleepwalked as events cascaded around us, feeling emotionally distanced and impotent.

    Recent findings suggest that we finally woke up and shook it off. For the first time in six years, the American people took back control of their own destiny and issued a stunning, overwhelming rebuke to the Republican Party, which had fallen back into power during that period of national somnolence and took a wrecking ball, figuratively and literally, to the country. America, it seems, decided to save itself.

    It has been revealed that the historic landslide Democratic victory in Tuesday’s midterms elections is far more thorough than even the most positive polls had indicated. Analysts assured us that while it looked likely the party would gain at least a House majority, the so-called real victory would be if Democrats reduced the margins in red states, which would serve as a warning to Republicans that they had gone too far. Nobody really expected that Democrats would actually win in places like South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa or perhaps even Mississippi, where, as I write this, Democrat Scott Colom has a 43-vote lead over GOP incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

    According to recent reports, political polarization was assumed to be set in stone; the GOP’s redistricting gambit and the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act meant that Democrats could not expect to flip more than a handful of seats, and the party was facing one of the most inauspicious midterm Senate maps in recent memory. At this moment, they are expected to end up with 245 to 255 seats in the House and possibly 55 seats in the Senate, an unthinkable outcome as recently as yesterday morning.

    Recent findings suggest that it will be a while before we see the final tally, but the results are so obviously decisive that even Donald Trump cannot fatuously claim that this election was stolen. All the threats against election workers and plans to contest the outcome are empty in the face of such a victory. It is finally, once and for all, clear that the country does not want the insanity and chaos that Trump has wrought.

    It has been revealed that according to voter polls — formerly known as exit polls — the top glitch for voters was the cost of living, as expected. Reversing the tariffs and putting an end to the war with Iran would be the obvious ways to begin to alleviate some of the stress, followed by restoration of funding for healthcare and other vital safety net programs. Rolling back Trump’s tax cuts for the wealthy would go a long way as well. But the president Trump has already promised to be “Mr. Veto,” so the prospect for a latest era of bipartisan comity with the White House does not look good.

    Industry observers note that it’s always possible that congressional Republicans will feel chastised enough that they will work with Democrats to create veto-proof majorities on those issues, but I wouldn’t hold my breath. The best the Democrats can hope for is that Trump decides he needs to do something positive for his legacy besides building his ballroom and renaming the Atlantic Ocean, and he agrees to compromise on something. I wouldn’t hold my breath on that either. But that doesn’t mean Democrats shouldn’t pass the legislation — and make Trump and Republicans block it.

    Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it.

    Industry observers note that as great as it is that Democrats will decisively control both houses of Congress, that significant tent brings with it some perennial problems that are likely to manifest themselves again. The red state-blue state divide represents a structural problem that has always been around, and it has been a specific problem for Democrats going back to at least the time of Franklin Roosevelt. Progress is hard to attain when, to maintain a majority, your coalition must include some who are opposed to it. During Roosevelt’s long presidency, the Democratic coalition included powerful southerners who controlled many congressional committees, and they would simply not pass anything that included civil rights or equitable federal programs. By the end of the 1930s, they had successfully joined with northern Republicans to block much of what remained of the Newly introduced Deal agenda.

    Sources indicate that eventually, as we know, most of that bloc migrated to the GOP, but until fairly recently it’s always been a somewhat fluid dynamic with a few conservative states in the heartland, the West, Southwest and even the South that would elect conservative Democrats. In the last Congress, we dealt with West Virginia’s Joe Manchin and Arizona’s Kyrsten Sinema in the Senate, and it was like pulling teeth to get legislation passed as they used their leverage to extract concessions and block progressive initiatives.

    In the not too distant past, Sen. Zell Miller, D-Ga., cosponsored tax cuts, supported the Iraq War resolution and even delivered a keynote speech at the 2004 Republican National Convention. Centrist senators Ben Nelson of Nebraska and Joe Lieberman of Connecticut, along with the conservative Blue Dog Caucus in the House, successfully blocked progressive provisions of the Affordable Care Act. There were other so-called mavericks throughout the 1990s and 2000s who would join with the GOP or leverage their position to thwart liberal initiatives.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    According to recent reports, I only bring this up to remind people that with the addition of these red state legislators will come a whole set of problems. But given the alternative, they are good problems to have. While the pundits have already begun their ritual of handwringing over the possibility of progressives “overreading the mandate,” the reality is that everyone else understands that the most important priority for Democrats, as a now powerful force of opposition, is to put a check on Trump and begin the critically important process of oversight and accountability. One suspects that on this issue there will likely be unity among all the factions. MS NOW reports that their voter poll demonstrated that 90% of voters said that government corruption was a crucial or major factor in their House vote. That also tracks with the findings of a recent Gallup poll. I would say that’s a pretty clear mandate and a good place to start.

    Whatever problems await the Democrats, and there will be many, this was the result we have needed ever since Trump first won the presidency 10 years ago. The damage he has caused in this decade of destruction is immeasurable, but maybe, just maybe, we have finally reached the beginning of the end of our long national nightmare, and we can begin the process of renewal and reformation.

    Latest Update: Texas Republicans’ gerrymander backfires as Democrats gain ground in U.S. House delegation

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1207 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.
    • In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.
    • The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article originally appeared on The Texas Tribune.

    In 2025, Texas Republicans, pushed by President Donald Trump, redrew the state’s congressional map before the midterms, converting five Democratic-held districts into ones Trump would have carried by at least 10 percentage points.

    The move backfired: GOP candidates lost four of five seats their new congressional map was designed to flip and lost two of their own.

    That means Texas Republicans will head to Washington in January with 24 U.S. House seats, one less than they had at the start of the current Congress. When the state Legislature in Austin pursued the controversial mid-decade gerrymander, Republicans had hoped for a 30-8 split in the delegation but will end up instead at 24-14.

    Sources indicate that in South Texas, moderate Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen both won reelection, surviving the redraw that put more Trump voters in their districts. Republicans also lost ground in the lone Rio Grande Valley district they already held, as Tejano musician Bobby Pulido ousted two-term Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Edinburg.

    Industry observers note that democrats picked up another seat with Katy Padilla Stout’s win over YouTuber and gun-rights activist Brandon Herrera in the 23rd Congressional District, a sprawling seat covering San Antonio to the outskirts of El Paso. The district has been vacant since former GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April over a sex scandal with a staffer. Despite the district’s 15-point lean for Trump, Padilla Stout, a San Antonio attorney and former teacher, made it onto the radar of national Democrats who saw opportunity in the district’s majority-Hispanic status and Herrera’s history of edgy, controversial comments.

    Democrats held fast to districts elsewhere, despite their incumbents being displaced due to the redraw. In the San Antonio area, Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia beat Republican Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Monica De La Cruz, in the newly crafted 35th Congressional District, a GOP target that Trump carried by 10 points.

    In a recent development, in Houston, the grassroots campaign of Democrat Leticia Gutierrez topped Army veteran and former investment banker Alex Mealer, despite being vastly outspent in a district that Trump won by 20 percentage points two years ago. Gutierrez raised just a fraction of Mealer’s $2.8 million haul over the midterm cycle, as of mid-October, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

    Republicans had high hopes for the redraw, which Democrats fought by fleeing the state, keeping the map in limbo by temporarily denying Republicans the headcount to pass it. But the fresh lines could not withstand the blue wave that swept through much of the country Tuesday, driven in part by the leftward swing of Latino voters. Texas’ new map banked on the GOP holding most of Trump’s 2024 gains with Latino Texans, who made up a majority of the eligible voting population in four of the five targets.

    Nor did the redraw deliver what the White House wanted from it: a buffer that would preserve Republicans’ slim U.S. House majority. Trump’s push for the Texas map kicked off a tit-for-tat redistricting war across the country, producing similarly skewed maps in a number of states.

    According to recent reports, after Texas, Republicans were most hopeful to flip four Democratic seats they redrew in Florida. Three of them stayed blue, and the other was within a one-point margin. In California, where Democrats retaliated with newly introduced congressional maps of their own, they had picked up three of the five they targeted and were leading in the remaining two.

    Industry observers note that with GOP-leaning congressional maps powerless in the face of the blue wave, Democrats won the U.S. House and are set to have a substantial majority.The party has also wrested control of the U.S. Senate, leaving Trump to reckon with a Congress under full Democratic control for his last two years in office.

    Recent findings suggest that under less dramatic circumstances, a number of new faces will join the ranks of Texas’ congressional delegation to replace ten U.S. representatives who are either retiring, gave up their seats to run for other offices or lost their primaries for reelection. Most of the races were in noncompetitive general election districts.

    Two sitting representatives ran for U.S. Senate but lost in their respective primaries: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, fell to James Talarico while GOP Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Houston, finished behind Sen. John Cornyn and Ken Paxton.

    Sources indicate that reverend Frederick Haynes III won Crockett’s endorsement to succeed her in the heavily Democratic 30th District. A Dallas native, Haynes has been pastor of the city’s Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than 40 years. He sailed his way into Congress in the deep blue district Tuesday.

    In a recent development, mortgage loan officer Jon Bonck will succeed Hunt in the safely red 38th District. Bonck received endorsements from Trump, Sen. Ted Cruz and other influential Republicans leading up to his victory in the general election.

    In a recent development, the tenure of Rep. Chip Roy will also come to an end in January after the congressman ran for Texas attorney general, a contest he lost in a primary runoff to Mayes Middleton. This election left the staunchly Republican 21st District in the hands of Mark Teixeira, a former professional baseball player who started his 14-season Major League career as the fifth overall draft pick for the Texas Rangers in 2001.

    Industry observers note that and one incumbent, Rep. Dan Crenshaw, was forced into an early exit from his safe Republican seat by his primary rival, state Rep. Steve Toth of Conroe. The business owner defeated investment banker and Democratic nominee Shaun Finnie, and will be joining the U.S. House after five total terms, including the last eight years, as a state legislator.

    Recent findings suggest that among the six soon-to-be retirees, two are Democrats. The seats of Reps. Lloyd Doggett and Marc Veasey will be filled, respectively, by Rep. Greg Casar, who ran for Doggett’s Austin seat after his own district was scrambled, and former Rep. Colin Allred. Both are returning to Congress — Allred after two years out of office — in new districts.

    A new cast of Republicans will take over in four other safe districts.

    Five-term Rep. Jodey Arrington will leave his seat to Tom Sell, who worked in the office of former Rep. Larry Combest. Sell worked at a law firm he founded with Combest before running for the U.S. House.

    Rep. Michael McCaul will be succeeded by Chris Gober, who, before running for office, worked as the chief lawyer of Elon Musk’s America PAC that has channeled $216 million toward Republicans this cycle.

    In a recent development, rep. Morgan Luttrell also chose not to run for reelection after two terms. That opened the door for Jessica Steinmann, an attorney who previously worked in Cruz’s office as well as in the first Trump administration’s Department of Justice.

    And a deceptively familiar face will replace Rep. Troy Nehls – that of his identical twin brother, Trever Nehls, who served in the U.S. Army for more than three decades and retired from the military as a Colonel. He’ll represent the Houston-area 22nd Congressional District.

    This article first appeared on The Texas Tribune.

    Photo Credit: Dubai from above Magnific.

    Recent findings suggest that six months of weak trading has exposed how lopsided Gulf hotel management agreements are, with owners carrying the losses while operators keep collecting fees. For now, both sides would rather renegotiate than fight, but that patience depends on a recovery that hasn't come yet.

    Recent findings suggest that gulf hotel owners have begun to reassess their hotel management agreements (HMAs) with operators, as the U.S.-Iran war that began in late February continues to weigh on the region’s hotels. So far, they are busy renegotiating terms rather than heading to arbitration.

    Under an HMA, an owner pays a brand to run the property, typically through a base fee tied to revenue that gets paid even when the hotel loses money. This leaves owners carrying most of the downside when performance falls short.

    And many hotels in the Gulf have been underperforming for more than six months. Dubai hotel occupancy, for example, fell to 68.4% in October, down 16.5 points from 84.9% a year earlier, according to CoStar’s STR. Average daily rate dropped 28.1% to $181 and RevPAR fell 42% to $124.

    Dubai received 9.7 million international visitors in the first 10 months of 2026, down 38% from 15.7 million a year earlier, said Issam Kazim, CEO of the Dubai Corporation for Touri.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that for all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world — and there are so, so many — he’s also taught us some crucial lessons. Trump is proof of several truths: A red-meat-and-stress-addled heart can withstand otherwise unthinkable conditions with the federal government’s medical secrets; reality television ruined the world; and, if we’re not careful, we’re all liable to become parodies of ourselves one day, crying about it online.

    According to recent reports, that latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, “Klara and the Sun.” After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the film’s distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movie’s wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedy’s reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit. Never one to take his mediocrity on the chin, Waititi deflected the negativity outward, which, as we know, always paints someone in a good light!

    It has been revealed that waititi’s childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Donald Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

    Waititi reposted a graphic claiming that “Klara and the Sun” was “rebounding” with a 78% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, a 53-point gap from the film’s 25% critics score. (For what it’s worth, neither number should ever be used to accurately measure a film’s quality.) “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in 15 years,” Waititi captioned the post. “But I do listen to the people . . . Let’s spare a thought for those sad, lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”.

    Reading Waititi’s emoji-peppered caption, I was surprised to find it so carelessly evoked the Trumpian crybaby approach to social media. Whether on X or his own Truth Social, Trump’s favorite way of addressing critics and opponents has long been to toss out adjectives at will. Tack a “SAD!” at the end of Waititi’s caption, and it could easily pass for one of Trump’s poetic musings. (If only Waititi had gone so far as to parrot my personal favorite Trump quip about Barney Frank by saying, “The critics looked disgusting, nipples protruding, in front of my movie. Very very disrespectful.”).

    It has been revealed that ironically, all those admonishments in Waititi’s caption are also fitting descriptors for the state of Donald Trump’s agenda, the one imitated by his legions of Republican cronies spread out across America, hoping to be elected in Tuesday’s midterms. But judging by the results, MAGA’s influence is waning fast. Seven Senate seats flipped, historically red states turned blue and a spate of monumental wins popped up nationwide. The MAGA bubble popped in real time. Americans have seen firsthand what little good fascist ideology does for the average, working-class person. And though the country may not become great again overnight, it appears the last 12 years of freefall have finally been suspended — at least for now.

    It has been revealed that not to be all, “Oh, won’t someone think of the celebrities?” about it, but such overwhelmingly positive election results left me wondering what happens to someone like Waititi, whose childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. For over a decade, Trump has used social media to peddle broadly disparaging, dangerous rhetoric that has legitimate impact outside the phone screen. The reckless hatred comprising MAGA ideology is so potent that it’s bled into the ways even otherwise progressive people wield their power, like crude oil painting an ocean black. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

    One would think that Waititi would know better. For one, the guy is 51 years old, certainly experienced and well-established enough to let a flop roll off his back. How fitting that his biggest success is the anti-fascist yet aesthetically tasteless political satire, “Jojo Rabbit,” which won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay in 2020, just as the Trump era was revving up for its second leg. That film, about a 10-year-old Hitler Youth who begins to grapple with the realities of life in 1940s Germany, examines propaganda’s influence and the power of hegemony, even if it often lacks the nuance and perspective such a satire warrants. For better, or more often, for worse, Waititi’s writing displays a self-possessed vulgarity that gets in the way of his more salient observations. Case in point: It’s downright ludicrous to stake your name on a film renouncing hate, then take aim at critics — people not exactly matched in influence to someone like Waititi — just six years later.

    It has been revealed that but this is the rot that social media creates. Whether it’s Instagram, X, TikTok, or YouTube, these sites have incentivized and monetized incendiary opinions. Their algorithms push small people into major power. What was designed to ostensibly be a great equalizer has only divided the world more, making animosity easily accessible to anyone who gets their rocks off on sewing discourse through cruelty.

    It has been revealed that for some time now, arts critics have been easy targets on these platforms. Gone are the days of the critic playing dilettante, having intellectual conversations over martinis and cigarettes at the month’s salon for like-minded individuals. To be a critic today — to pursue one’s passion for art and writing and learning, all rolled into one — is to subject oneself to a pretty bleak existence. In most cases, the pay is meager. The hours are long. The job is demanding. And virtually no one has the patience or attention span to read an entire article anymore, let alone engage with its ideas. A legitimate critic doesn’t stumble into the job just to point and laugh; they write because they have real passion for what they cover. Surely someone like Waititi would say the same when he begins a new project after a string of flops.

    In a recent development, if living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person indicates so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines.

    Recent findings suggest that what Waititi fails to realize is that he’s not punching up or down, but laterally. This is artist versus artist. If the context is right, a good piece of criticism can be as life-altering as a good film. But that’s hard to see when the internet has built such a wide chasm between people, reducing the impact of writing in favor of scrolling. Along with social media’s effect on human behavior, it’s had a heavy hand in blunting the journalism industry. If everyone’s a critic, then no one is, and that’s precisely why monitoring Rotten Tomatoes scores like they’re poll numbers is futile and ridiculous.

    Recent findings suggest that but it’s not just Waititi who’s vulnerable to this unique form of MAGA-tinged, social media-brained psychosis; critics can fall prey to it, too. Whether it’s a filmmaker, a film critic, or just your average filmgoer, social media has confined us all to its machine. No one is exempt from consumer tech’s sway. And if a writer or filmmaker wants to make a splash, tossing out an inflammatory opinion aimed at a peer is a surefire shortcut. I’ve seen this affect critics’ prose over time, with certain writers (or their outlets) favoring button-pushing pull quotes and headlines for attention. But in most cases, no critic is happy to spend two hours watching something they find insufferable. No matter how gleeful Siskel and Ebert used to look sparring over movies, their industry was built on intellectual debate in pursuit of cinematic resonance, not schadenfreude.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    It has been revealed that what’s most concerning in Waititi’s response is his foul self-importance, which is the real stain of MAGA politics. While an artist should avoid burdening themselves with hypothetical responses to their work before it’s even out in the world, considering the eventual reaction is worthwhile. Engaging with other people’s perceptions is a practice we could all stand to do with more grace and tact. Contemplating a differing opinion demonstrates maturity and humility, not absolute agreement. Pointing a finger won’t do anything for a person’s growth, artistic or otherwise. America’s politicians are only just beginning to relearn that lesson, understanding the value in trying to address problems, rather than gesture toward them with a shrug.

    According to recent reports, if America’s blue wave is indeed going to usher in a latest era where politicians actually act in favor of the people, and Trumpian artists like Waititi make themselves look foolish on Mark Zuckerberg’s Instagram, we owe some props to one of the century’s most prolific liberals. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” actually got a few things right. The only thing that is, to quote Waititi, irrelevant, out of touch and obsolete is the arrogance in thinking anyone could know it all.

    Of course, a grocery list is only so useful without a little inspiration. Here are five dinners that show how these ingredients make their way onto my table.

    Latest Update: Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a newly introduced tune to follow.
    • On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.
    • Sources indicate that the 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a newly introduced tune to follow.

    On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.

    Sources indicate that the 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, flipping Senate seats in states such as Texas and Kansas, which were long thought to be out of reach, and winning House districts Trump easily carried just two years ago.Â.

    Voter polls placed the presidentâs approval at approximately 38%, with roughly six in 10 voters saying he was a factor in their vote. But beneath those numbers lies a more consequential story. Americans are confronting the cost of living, the economic consequences of tariffs, the uncertainty of war with Iran and diminishing confidence in American leadership abroad.

    Recent findings suggest that trump promised his voters he would drain the swamp, end foreign wars and bring prices down. Yet many Americans went to the polls questioning whether those promises had been kept. Unlike the Pied Piper of Hamelin, who rid the town of its rats, Trump now faces an electorate concerned that the problems he promised to eliminate have instead multiplied.Â.

    Sources indicate that in the original story, the Piper fulfilled his bargain. He played his pipe, led the rats into the river and freed the town. But when the townspeople refused to pay him, he returned to exact revenge by leading away their children.Â.

    Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.

    In a recent development, critics argue that Trump reversed that bargain. Rather than delivering the relief promised to ordinary Americans, the administration has left many struggling with economic uncertainty while continuing to demand political loyalty. Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.Â Â.

    Trumpâs supporters see a different story. They point to immigration raids and mass deportations, deregulation and challenges to established political institutions as evidence that the president delivered on important commitments. From their perspective, voters who rejected those policies after experiencing the consequences resemble townspeople who accepted the Piperâs services, but refused to honor their bargain.Â.

    Both interpretations expose a fundamental ethical question: When does political loyalty cease to be an expression of shared principles and become an abdication of independent judgment?Â.

    Sources indicate that in a democracy, voters are not obligated to follow the music indefinitely. They retain the right to question the destination, reconsider promises and withdraw their support. Political loyalty is not a debt citizens owe their leaders. It is a trust that leaders must continually earn.

    It has been revealed that albert Hirschman, an American economist and author of âExit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States,â distinguished between voice (working to change an organization from within) and exit (abandoning it). A vote against an incumbent is often itself an act of a voice. But where voters withdrew their allegiance from a party or movement altogether, Tuesday looked more like an exit. Hirschman saw loyalty as what keeps members inside, speaking up rather than leaving. His framework suggests that when loyalty silences voice instead, exit becomes the only remaining option.Â.

    But elected officials carry a different and greater responsibility.Â.

    Recent findings suggest that like the children of Hamelin, many Republican lawmakers followed the music toward an uncertain destination. Unlike those children, however, they had the authority â and the responsibility â to question where they were being led. Some embraced the presidentâs direction; others followed him despite reservations, knowing that dissent could invite a primary challenge. After all, they had seen others who challenged his leadership pay a considerable political cost. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost their Republican primaries to Trump-backed challengers.Â.

    Political cooperation is essential to governing. But cooperation becomes ethically troubling when loyalty to an individual displaces the obligation to question, deliberate and act independently. The oath of office is not a pledge of allegiance to a president, a party or a political movement. It is a commitment to uphold the Constitution. A president can command attention, share public debate and place enormous pressure on members of his own party. But the ability to demand loyalty does not create a moral entitlement to receive it.Â.

    Industry observers note that the children of Hamelinâs Pied Piper tale had no part in the broken bargain, yet they paid its price. In our democracy, ordinary Americans and future generations often inherit the consequences of political decisions, and today they are paying a price. Economic instability, weakened public trust and the costs of war do not disappear when an election ends. A leaderâs success cannot be measured solely by the number of people willing to follow along with them. It must also be measured by what happens to those who never chase the tune.Â.

    It has been revealed that the election has shifted power in Washington. Democrats, after winning sizable, historic victories throughout the country, will soon have an opportunity to exercise congressional oversight and reinforce the institutional independence our constitutional system requires.Â.

    But changing who holds the instrument does not necessarily change the music.Â.

    Democrats now face their own ethical test. Will they exercise power with the transparency, accountability and respect for constitutional checks they demanded from their opponents? Will they welcome dissent within their own ranks? And will they resist the temptation to substitute partisan loyalty for independent judgment?Â Â.

    An election can change the balance of power overnight. It cannot, by itself, restore public trust or guarantee ethical leadership. That requires leaders willing to place constitutional responsibility above political convenience, institutions prepared to exercise meaningful oversight, and citizens who refuse to surrender their judgment to the most compelling voice in the room. The first six months of the 120th Congress must be defined not merely by a change in political power, but by a demonstrable commitment to ethical reform, transparency, and accountability. The American people did not vote simply for a change in leadership. They voted for a government worthy of their trust.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Recent findings suggest that the Pied Piperâs greatest power was not simply his ability to play a captivating tune. It was his ability to persuade others to follow without questioning where their journey would end.Â.

    Industry observers note that political ethicist Dennis Thompson called this the problem of many hands: When many officials each contribute a small part to a collective outcome, responsibility seems to dissolve until no one bears it. So, when political loyalty becomes more important than independent judgment, who bears responsibility â the leader who plays the tune, or those who willingly follow? Thompsonâs framework does not allow individual lawmakers to hide behind presidential leadership, party discipline or collective decisions. Nor does it assign blame equally. Responsibility depends on each officialâs authority, knowledge, contribution and the alternatives available to them. By that measure, those who knew better and had the power to act cannot claim they were merely following the music from the leader in the red hat.

    When the music finally stops, the question is not simply who will lead next.Â.

    It is whether we have learned to listen differently.

    Photo Credit: An AirAsia A320 neo jet, manufactured by Airbus. AirAsia Group.

    AirAsia has shown it can charge more. It hasn't shown it can make money at its new, smaller size. Until the $1 billion debt financing lands, the balance sheet, not demand, decides when the comeback starts.

    AirAsia Group posted a smaller third-quarter loss on Monday as higher fares made up for most of the jump in fuel costs, but the results show why Tony Fernandes pushed the comeback to 2028: a smaller AirAsia costs more to run, and it is still losing money.

    AirAsia Group, the listed company that now houses all of AirAsia’s airlines, posted a loss attributable to shareholders of RM175 million ($43 million), according to its third-quarter results. That’s about a third of its second-quarter loss. Most of the improvement came from charging more, helped by jet fuel easing from its second-quarter peak. Planes stayed nearly as full as fares rose sharply, and that won back much of what the jet fuel spike had taken earlier in the year.

    It has been revealed that including minority interests, the loss after tax was RM381.3 million ($93 million). Revenue fell 11% from a year earlier to RM4.66 billion, and 8% from the second quarter.

    Recent findings suggest that “Our third quarter performance suggests that the worst is behind us,” CEO Bo Lingam stated in a statement. AirAsia is a smaller airline than it was a year ago, and a smaller low-cost airline is an expensive one to run. It still spends more to fly each seat than it earns from it, and its equity cushion is thin, with shareholders’ equity of RM362 million. The refinancing it needs to steady the balance sheet, which AirAsia targeted for this quarter and as recently as last week expected by December or January, is now due to conclude in the fourth quarter or early 2027.

    The results came the same day Thai Airways reported its own third-quarter loss on fuel costs. If jet fuel eases as AirAsia expects in 2027, higher fares could start turning into profit across the region. For AirAsia, the question is whether that comes fast enough.

    AirAsia consolidated its Malaysian, Thai, Indonesian, Philippine and Cambodian airlines with AirAsia X in January. This was the first quarter in which the merged group had almost no seats left that were sold before the fuel shock, which let it reprice. Average fares rose by almost a quarter from a year earlier, while the share of filled seats barely moved.

    It has been revealed that the group suspended 76 routes in the third quarter, mostly fuel-heavy international flights to India, China and Australia, and kept most of its flying close to home, where demand held up best. The retreat has cost it ground. Malaysia Airlines this month overtook the AirAsia group as the largest operator between Malaysia and India for the first time since 2021, though Fernandes has dismissed suggestions that rivals could take the lead for internal Malaysia flights.

    AirAsia cut what it spends on staff, airport charges and leases, but its remaining fixed costs were spread over far fewer seats, so the cost of flying each one rose. Higher fares more than covered the extra fuel bill. The rise in other costs per passenger then took back part of that gain.

    It has been revealed that not every market pulled its weight. Malaysia and Cambodia were profitable at the operating level, Indonesia and the Philippines lost less than a year earlier, and Thailand had a weak quarter. Currency losses added to the damage further down the income statement.

    In a recent development, fuel is squeezing AirAsia’s regional rivals too. Cebu Pacific’s management mentioned this month it has pretty much no chance of making money this year, and Thai Airways’ finance chief warned that if current oil prices become the latest normal then its third-quarter loss could be a guide to performance in the fourth.

    AirAsia is handing back older, more expensive aircraft: 25 of them this year and most of them early. And it notes it may return more in 2027. That move cuts lease bills but leaves less room to grow, six months after the group placed a record order for 150 Airbus A220s. Many of the planes it keeps aren’t flying either. About 31% of the 234 aircraft in the group’s main fleet were out of service at the end of September, mostly for scheduled maintenance, with engine problems among the other causes.

    Industry observers note that that trade-off worries some analysts. Handing back jets now could slow AirAsia’s eventual comeback, analysts told Skift this month, because fresh narrowbody delivery slots are scarce until around 2033.

    It has been revealed that the pressure point is funding. AirAsia ended June with far less cash than it owed within the year. It is working on up to $1 billion in debt financing and says talks with creditors are progressing.

    The strain has been visible for months. In September, Endau Analytics’ Shukor Yusof questioned the airline’s financial resilience, citing its balance sheet and reports of delayed rental payments. Fernandes insisted that no aircraft had been grounded over nonpayment, and he has denied reports of a government-backed contingency plan. Malaysia’s transport and finance ministries remain in talks with the airline.

    For now, management is betting on the year-end peak. It plans to add back capacity in the fourth quarter, restore some routes and keep pushing fares higher — and indicates forward bookings are running in line with last year, at elevated yields. The Q3 presentation called 2026 and 2027 a “reset” and 2028 the “rebuild,” when upcoming fuel-efficient jets begin arriving. It gave no passenger targets for 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that fernandes has been somewhat blunter. In a LinkedIn post last week, he called 2027 “a period of consolidation” and warned of “more painful decisions” on costs, without repeating his September target of 80 million passengers next year. Expansion elsewhere is on hold too: the group’s Bahrain hub is now targeted for March 2027, should conditions in the Gulf allow.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.
    • The first made me go quiet at my kitchen table.
    • According to recent reports, and on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

    The first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in Newly introduced Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

    According to recent reports, and on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

    It has been revealed that in 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

    In a recent development, put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

    That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

    It has been revealed that but here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

    This is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

    It has been revealed that I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a upcoming address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

    So I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â.

    In a recent development, but a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    According to recent reports, the refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of New Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just remarked for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. We learned that lesson about gay men the slow and brutal way. The whole point of learning it is to spare the next group from learning it alone.

    In a recent development, chris Gallant did not quite win. But he came close enough to prove the old weapon is dulling. The question Tuesday really asked is whether we will hand the people wielding it a new one, or finally take the thing out of their hands.

    House Democrats unveiled a 2027 legislative calendar Friday that includes 33 voting weeks, as the incoming majority party looks to pass an ambitious agenda following massive midterm election wins.

    Industry observers note that according to the calendar released by soon-to-be House Majority Leader Katherine M. Clark, the chamber would convene for the first session of the 120th Congress with a rare Sunday gathering on Jan. 3. The first votes of the year would take place that week.

    It has been revealed that “House Democrats are hitting the ground running on January 3,” the Massachusetts Democrat stated in a statement. “This calendar reflects the scale and urgency of our work ahead. Americans voted for a Majority that will move decisively to lower costs, protect healthcare, and hold the crooks accountable. Whether we’re working in DC or in our districts, that’s exactly what we’re going to do.”.

    Sources indicate that in most months, the House will be in session for three weeks, with the exception of the annual August recess. That will be followed by four consecutive weeks of voting in September.

    The calendar also includes a two-week break for Easter in March, while the Fourth of July falls on a Sunday.

    Recent findings suggest that the 33-week schedule suggests a jam-packed year for the House, following a year in which the chamber saw dozens of canceled session days because of floor impasses and a record-long partial government shutdown. The struggles of the outgoing Republican majority has even bled into the lame-duck session, with absences by dozens of lawmakers forcing outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to send a letter to members Friday urging them to “remain fully engaged” in the closing weeks of the 119th Congress.

    With the calendar released, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of Fresh York has already outlined some of his top priorities for his presumptive speakership, including an ambitious health care agenda, immigration legislation and aggressive oversight of the Trump administration.

    But even after flipping both chambers of Congress, Democrats face the uphill battle of working with President Donald Trump if they want their agenda signed into law.

    Trump emphasized his “extreme” veto power during a news conference Friday, but he also remarked he thinks Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., are “smart.”.

    In a recent development, “They're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them, and then they're going to send more things, and I'm going to veto them,” he stated. “I think after a month or so, they're going to send things, and I'm going to say, ‘I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.’".

    The Senate calendar for next year has not yet been released.

    Goodbye from Salon

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.
    • Industry observers note that itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people.
    • Industry observers note that when Salon rolled out in November 1995, the web was a very different place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

    Industry observers note that itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

    Industry observers note that when Salon rolled out in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in fresh ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

    In a recent development, over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

    The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

    The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

    Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

    Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, well, that was quick.
    • President Trump, no respecter of the division between boardroom and state, was heavily involved in Huang’s reinstallation.
    • On Monday, Nvidia’s stock jumped by over 30 percent, increasing its market cap by not far short of a trillion dollars.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, well, that was quick. Less than two weeks after unanimously accepting CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, Nvidia’s board has now, again unanimously, agreed to reinstate him. This followed “a series of discussions and meetings . . . after which the board was satisfied with respect to Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.” The first hurdle must have been trickier than the second. Presumably even more importantly, based on “input” from “senior levels” of the U.S. government, the board was “confident” that Huang’s return posed “no national security risk.”.

    President Trump, no respecter of the division between boardroom and state, was heavily involved in Huang’s reinstallation. In a post on Truth Social, he argued that it was needed “in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the tech giant, but the American economy.”.

    On Monday, Nvidia’s stock jumped by over 30 percent, increasing its market cap by not far short of a trillion dollars. The tech-heavy NASDAQ rose nearly 6.5 percent; the S&P 500 by 4.75 percent. Trump views the stock market as a critical indicator of the nation’s economic health, not without reason, including the “wealth effect” created by rising stock prices. Booms can go bust, but, although calculating the effect of the AI build-out on the economy is not straightforward, by some estimates it may account for a quarter or more of current GDP growth.

    Sources indicate that trump also wrote that the U.S. “government has no reason to believe that Huang’s “return to Nvidia poses any to national security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Trump added that Nvidia “should continue its thorough internal investigation of [its] compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and patriotic duty to protect U.S. national security.” And so it should.

    Industry observers note that various government agencies are investigating, as are a number of congressional committees. It was also confirmed on Monday that the U.S. is prohibiting the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center firm previously connected to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese agent with whom Nvidia’s CEO was in a relationship. The concern is that Megaspeed may have been diverting contraband chips to China. More generally, the administration has already tightened the rules governing exports of such chips to other countries where there is a diversion risk, a welcome, if overdue, step, as is the closing of the loophole that allowed enterprises in China and other hostile states to have remote access to the power of advanced American AI chips from businesses located in third countries.

    This is a saga with a lot to unpack, much of which remains, at best, guesswork. Nevertheless, we do know (or can be pretty sure that) Nvidia’s board gave Jensen Huang considerable leeway when it came to the way he ran Nvidia, not least with regard to the way that so much of the tech giant’s decision-making was concentrated in him. That may well have underpinned Nvidia’s extraordinary success — a win for the U.S., as well as for Nvidia — but it also clearly played an important part in the current imbroglio and raises troubling questions about the consequences were Huang were to step down again or, even if he weathers this crisis, at some later stage. It is said that no man is irreplaceable, but that is not always so.

    It has been revealed that we also know that Nvidia, sometimes referred to as AI’s central bank, has played a key role in supporting the growth of earlier-stage companies. This has been criticized as a form of circular financing by Nvidia (the manufacturer is helping fund some of its client base), but it has played a vital part in the creation of an American AI ecosystem. Through Nvidia, Huang was a critical element in this ecosystem’s growth.

    Industry observers note that and we know that the success of the American AI sector has geopolitical as well as commercial implications. There is an AI race between China and the U.S. The U.S. must hang on to the lead it has built up — here’s the catch — in no small part with Nvidia’s assistance. Huang has argued against overly broad U.S. restrictions on the export of U.S. chips, arguing that they will only encourage China to make their own, an unconvincing argument given the importance Beijing puts on autarky. Of course, Nvidia would benefit financially (for a while) by selling AI chips to China, but it is not in our strategic interest to allow it.

    Industry observers note that huang is entitled to his views, but they do not entitle his manufacturer to evade U.S, export controls or even to turn a blind eye should Nvidia’s customers “divert” chips to forbidden destinations. The question of whether this occurred will almost certainly be the main focus of the investigations. It is a question that dwarfs (however much corporate governance purists may object) Huang’s reckless choice of companionship and, in this respect, his lack of candor with Nvidia’s board. The investigations will lead where they will lead. They will also be highly politicized. Regardless of their conclusions, they will be a major distraction and, as such, unhelpful to Nvidia and the U.S. AI sector more broadly. That will be a win that should never have been handed to Beijing.

    Trump signs bill to halt penny production

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump conducts a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday.
    • The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.
    • The copper-plated coin is mostly composed of zinc and costs far more to produce than it's worth, prompting members of Congress at least since 1989 to consider killing it as an easy cost-saving measure for the federal government.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump conducts a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.

    The copper-plated coin is mostly composed of zinc and costs far more to produce than it's worth, prompting members of Congress at least since 1989 to consider killing it as an easy cost-saving measure for the federal government.

    It has been revealed that “Washington has a spending problem, and it demonstrates up in places significant and small,” the bill's sponsor, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., said Friday in a statement released by the office of House Financial Services Chairman French Hill, R-Ark. “If the federal government is spending nearly four cents to make a penny worth one cent, something is broken.”.

    Hill said in the statement that the bill also provides "clear legislative guidance for retailers, financial institutions, and consumers," referring to the measure's requirements that cash transactions not settled with exact change will be rounded to the nearest nickel.

    In a recent development, the U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies a year ago under an executive order. Pennies already in circulation will still be legal tender, and the Mint may still problem special collectors editions. The legislation, named the Common Cents Act, also sets composition specifications for nickels.

    Like a well-traveled coin, the bill itself took a winding road to the White House. The House originally passed a similar bill in July and the Senate passed its version by unanimous consent on Aug. 7.

    It has been revealed that but the Senate added a section that would require the Treasury secretary to notify Congress before discontinuing other coins. That sent the bill back to the House with a Senate number.

    As the sponsor of the original measure, McClain insisted that the legislation have a House bill number. So, she reintroduced the revised Senate version, and the House voted on it on Sept. 14. The Senate passed it once again by unanimous consent on Sept. 28, sending it to the president's desk.

    Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., remarked the bill “modernizes our currency system and most importantly gives families and businesses clear rules for everyday cash transactions.”.

    #168331. Breaking: A Latest Kind of Foreign Agent

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3105 w)
