    ICJ Finds Myanmar Committed Genocide. What Comes Next?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that in August 2017, Myanmar’s military rolled out sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state.
    • Sources indicate that nine years later, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide.
    • Recent findings suggest that in August 2017, Myanmar’s military rolled out sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Recent findings suggest that in August 2017, Myanmar’s military rolled out sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state. Within just three months, security forces had killed thousands of people, razed hundreds of villages, committed widespread sexual violence, and forced some 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee into neighboring Bangladesh.

    Sources indicate that nine years later, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide. The landmark ruling, delivered Thursday, marked the first time that the United Nations’ top court has found a country directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

    Recent findings suggest that in August 2017, Myanmar’s military rolled out sweeping “clearance operations” against alleged insurgents in the country’s Rakhine state. Within just three months, security forces had killed thousands of people, razed hundreds of villages, committed widespread sexual violence, and forced some 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee into neighboring Bangladesh.

    Nine years later, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar guilty of genocide. The landmark ruling, delivered Thursday, marked the first time that the United Nations’ top court has found a country directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention.

    Industry observers note that foreign Policy spoke with Tom Andrews, the former U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in Myanmar, a few hours after the ruling came down. He discussed the decision’s implications, including where justice lies for the world’s largest stateless population and how the ruling could affect similar genocide cases linked to the wars in Gaza and Ukraine.

    This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

    Sources indicate that foreign Policy: Earlier today, the ICJ found that Myanmar’s security forces had committed genocide against the country’s minority Rohingya Muslim community. For those who aren’t aware of the case, could you give a brief primer on the court’s findings?

    Tom Andrews: They were very explicit in their findings. They talked about the thousands and thousands of people who were killed, the thousands of women who were raped, the more than 2,000 children who were killed, the hundreds of thousands of homes that were burned.

    Sources indicate that I was in Bangladesh when people had arrived [in 2017], and I sat and talked to many people who had literally been running for their lives. And the stories they told me were just absolutely incredible. I mean the horror, the brutality, the systematic nature of the killing, of the rapes, of the torture, was just absolutely extraordinary. And, of course, more than 700,000 people escaped into Bangladesh; we know that 1.3 million are now in Bangladesh, in the largest refugee camp in the world.

    But what [the Rohingya] did was they pushed for justice and they pushed for accountability. And there were people who were victimized by this brutality, who came to the court, the International Court of Justice, and provided their own personal testimony, told their own stories in a private session, which I believe was a very powerful, powerful part of this whole process, where it allowed the judges to focus on the actual consequences, the human element of this.

    Recent findings suggest that FP: This is the first time that the U.N.’s top court has found a nation directly responsible for genocide. What is the significance of that ruling?

    Recent findings suggest that TA: History was made today. The standard for genocide is very, very high. And that is a reason why this is so remarkable. This is the first time it’s ever been made, because the standard not only includes the acts but also the intention behind those acts—that [the state] designed to harm a population in whole or in part.

    But the question that it begs is, well, OK, now what? Now that we’ve established genocide, are there consequences for genocide, and what are they? And the court has ruled that the regime in Myanmar is responsible for providing relief and compensation for the victims.

    According to recent reports, I believe that that needs to occur both within the United Nations and outside of the United Nations. Within the United Nations, I believe that the United Nations Security Council should take this up. I think they should pass a resolution. I think that these individuals who were responsible for this genocide should be criminally prosecuted, and so there should be a reference to the International Criminal Court for that criminal prosecution.

    Sources indicate that I think it’s also key for us to recognize that the killings that continue to go on are happening because the military junta—the generals and [junta leader] Min Aung Hlaing—has access to sophisticated weapons of war that it’s using to attack civilians. I think it’s really important that the international community do everything that it can to cut off that access to those weapons and those weapon materials, and the financing that’s being used to acquire those weapons and those weapon materials, so that we can stop that flow.

    Industry observers note that another step that they can take is to reject this rehabilitation campaign that Min Aung Hlaing has been involved in now for the past few months. He’s been traveling to states in the region, to his neighbors, to ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] states. He’s been invited into these capitals, welcomed into these capitals. He’s been seeking to gain greater acceptance within ASEAN and the structure of ASEAN. And I think what’s really key is for those member states who have been moving in that direction of accepting or softening their relationship to Min Aung Hlaing and this genocidal regime to reverse those steps and that the regime be as isolated diplomatically as it deserves to be.

    FP: Do you think that the ruling will be enough, though, to actually push member states to take that next step and start to reverse the junta’s efforts to cast off its diplomatic pariah status?

    TA: I certainly hope so. I mean, this is unprecedented. This is a powerful, powerful moment for the world. I think it’s incredibly crucial for the world to respond to that finding in a responsible way and that member states and their citizens need to stand up and make their voices very, very clear and very strong that their government needs to do everything that it can to isolate this regime, weaken this regime, take away this regime’s capacity to continue to commit murder against its own people.

    I mean, this is a moral imperative, and it is a call for everyone to make a moral stand for not only the Rohingya, not only for the people of Myanmar, but for justice and humanity around the world. Because the thing is, if we establish that there is no consequence for genocide, then we can be guaranteed that genocide is going to happen again. And it’s only by imposing consequences that we can begin to see justice prevail, not only in this case but in future cases.

    In a recent development, FP: What’s next for the Rohingya community themselves? The ICJ doesn’t have an enforcement mechanism, but could this case have a tangible impact on the future of that population?

    Recent findings suggest that TA: It can, and it should. First of all, the world has turned its back on the Rohingya. Support for the conditions in which they’re living, the refugee camps, has been declining. There have been increased difficulties in just being able to survive in these camps, in part, certainly, by the fact of the international community reversing commitments that it had made and support that it provided to people who are in these conditions for no fault of their own.

    In a recent development, now, I think, with respect to reparations, the idea that the government of Myanmar—the current illegitimate regime of Myanmar—would accept the order of the court to provide compensation is, at best, a very, very remote possibility. In fact, I think that the chances of this happening are exactly zero. So, until there is a fresh regime that actually is legitimate and believes in justice and accountability and human rights, until that day happens, I think the world has to step forward, and I think there are options the world can take.

    Industry observers note that for example, the United Nations can establish a reparations fund and a mechanism to manage that. The United States, for example, seized over a billion dollars in assets from this regime. And that billion dollars can be used as part of a compensation fund, and that can then be built upon with governments coming forward to provide additional resources so that there is some form of justice and compensation for those who were victimized by these attacks.

    In a recent development, FP: What is the view coming out of Myanmar right now? Is there talk of this case possibly leading to something like regime change?

    TA: I’ve heard reports of additional hate speech that’s beginning to be drummed up, some of the nationalists that have used hate speech against the Rohingya in the past, that they are beginning to once again generate that kind of hatred against the Rohingya. It’s a dangerous moment in the country.

    FP: Obviously, this case has an outsized impact on Myanmar’s future, but could this ruling affect similar cases at the ICJ on the conflicts in Gaza and Ukraine?

    TA: It remains to be seen. The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations [Mike Waltz] posted a tweet in which—I’m paraphrasing here, but [he] accused the court of being poised to lower the standard for genocide, which could have an impact on future cases. And what’s happened is that the court was very explicit in saying that they used the current standard for genocide, including the standard of genocidal intent, in making this judgment. So, in fact, there was no lowering of the standard for genocide that some have accused the court of preparing to do.

    Sources indicate that I think what’s notable is to focus on this case, to focus on this community and on people who were wronged, and to focus on our responsibility to them and to accountability and justice for them and to make sure that there is a consequence for genocide. So I’m hoping that we’re not distracted by what might happen in the future, that we’re focused on what’s happening right now.

    According to recent reports, I saw a report that a child is killed in these attacks every 29 hours in Myanmar now. So, yes, we need to stop the atrocities from continuing, but we need to focus on responsibility and accountability for these acts and these acts of genocide.

    Democrats call for chip export and AI limits as Huang returns

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is among Democrats looking to take a harder line on AI and chip exports in the newly introduced year.
    • Incoming Democratic leaders called for tighter semiconductor export controls and investigations of the Trump administration Monday as Nvidia reinstated disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.
    • The problem also spilled into the party’s Senate majority leader election fight, as Democrats weigh plans to advance bills in the 120th Congress that would regulate artificial intelligence.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is among Democrats looking to take a harder line on AI and chip exports in the newly introduced year. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

    Incoming Democratic leaders called for tighter semiconductor export controls and investigations of the Trump administration Monday as Nvidia reinstated disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.

    The problem also spilled into the party’s Senate majority leader election fight, as Democrats weigh plans to advance bills in the 120th Congress that would regulate artificial intelligence.

    The reinstatement of Huang came as President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday the CEO “did nothing wrong” and that he had been “speaking to the [Nvidia] board directly and indirectly.”.

    Sources indicate that in a Monday statement, Nvidia noted its board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

    Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is challenging Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., for the majority leader role, told reporters Monday that in the “first 100 days” of the new Congress, he wants Senate rules changed to allow for faster floor consideration of bills that had broad bipartisan support in committee.

    He also supports legislation to require independent mandatory evaluations of AI systems and updates to liability laws to account not just for harm caused by AI models but for risks of internal development. He also mentioned a bill he sponsored that he said would ensure other electricity consumers don’t bear the costs of data center construction.

    Van Hollen also remarked that Congress should create a special joint committee on AI to consider the technology’s broader impacts, including on the workforce and economy.

    “I think we need to move urgently on the safety piece and then move with deliberation, but also speed, on tackling these other problems,” Van Hollen remarked.

    Industry observers note that last week, Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., wrote to Van Hollen and Schumer proposing a joint committee to “complement” the work of committees of jurisdiction and asking for their plans for AI if they were elected leader.

    Recent findings suggest that speaking to reporters and in his reply to Hickenlooper, Van Hollen also supported greater transparency into the AI industry’s financing and debt structure and tighter export controls on advanced chips like those sold by Nvidia. In particular, he said the Commerce Department should close “loopholes” for remote access to chips and purchase by affiliates of companies banned from directly acquiring sensitive technologies.

    Schumer, in a post on X Monday, noted Democrats would “work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries.”.

    “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Schumer wrote.

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., whose caucus officially backed him last week to be speaker in the fresh year, seconded the need for investigations into Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He also supported export controls.

    “The National Defense Authorization Act must include ironclad export control legislation to prevent powerful AI technology from being exploited by the Chinese Communist Party and other adversaries,” Jeffries wrote, referring to the pending fiscal 2027 defense policy bill.

    A manager’s amendment to the Senate’s version of the bill includes several chip export restrictions, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House-passed NDAA does not contain similar language.

    Meanwhile, Republican committee leaders pressed forward with intends to bring in Huang for questioning.

    It has been revealed that senate Banking Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., on Monday confirmed looks for a Dec. 3 hearing titled “Protecting America’s AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls” featuring Huang as a witness.

    Sources indicate that "Mr. Huang’s testimony before the Senate Banking Committee will be critical for protecting America’s AI advantage,” Scott said in a statement. “The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing.".

    Scott previously invited Lutnick to testify before the committee on Dec. 10.

    Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who looks likely to hold the banking gavel next Congress, said Huang’s return as CEO “only increases the urgency” of export controls.

    “The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the manufacturer’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Warren stated in a statement.

    House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., mentioned in a social media video on Monday that Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter would sit for transcribed interviews with his committee and with the House Intelligence Committee and Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party the week of Nov. 30.

    The committees also requested that Commerce Undersecretary for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler appear before the panels.

    Recent findings suggest that john T. Bennett contributed to this report.

    #168294. Why Israel Is Losing America

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2379 w)

    Why Israel Is Losing America

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2379 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress.
    • Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Key Ally.
    • American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    ANDREW P. MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress. He was Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Israeli-Palestinian Affairs in the Biden administration and Director for Egypt and Israel Military Complications on the National Security Council in the Obama administration.

    Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Key Ally.

    American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

    According to recent reports, as I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

    Things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a upcoming paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

    This change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

    Whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a fresh U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

    Sources indicate that trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

    In a recent development, time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace strategy for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is at the moment marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

    Moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he said himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

    Trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

    Recent findings suggest that trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

    Unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising latest ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

    Industry observers note that israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, revealed wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

    Industry observers note that israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

    According to recent reports, without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

    It is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

    Recent findings suggest that israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with fresh realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s strategy for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

    Sources indicate that israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

    Israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of new Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

    Israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

    These steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

    If Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Without access to international markets and capital, its economy, which has withstood the turmoil of the last several years remarkably well, will suffer and living standards will fall. Under these circumstances, Jewish Israeli citizens with second passports may elect to leave, depriving the state of its raison d’être—providing a safe and prosperous homeland for the Jewish people. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.

    What the Yalta Comparison Really Reveals About Shenzhen

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The moment that the trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, was planned, commentators began comparing it to the 1945 Yalta Conference.
    • According to recent reports, the Kremlin was right about the symbolism, not least because this week’s summit produced little else.
    • The moment that the trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, was planned, commentators began comparing it to the 1945 Yalta Conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    The moment that the trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, was planned, commentators began comparing it to the 1945 Yalta Conference. Unsurprisingly, this narrative was particularly fueled by Moscow, where the British-Soviet-U.S. “Massive Three” summit stands for the codification of Soviet control over half of Europe. Pyotr Tolstoy, the head of the foreign affairs committee in the Russian parliament, called the summit a “fresh Yalta.” Ultranationalist ideologue Alexander Dugin found the meeting “deeply symbolic,” while the Kremlin boasted that “the significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.”.

    According to recent reports, the Kremlin was right about the symbolism, not least because this week’s summit produced little else. The joint “Declaration Toward Peace” adopted by U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin states practically nothing. It pledges United Nations reform without specifics, future fuel shipments without volumes or deadlines, and a dialogue on nuclear risks without a clear path forward. Its most pointed passage is a warning to the International Criminal Court not to abuse its jurisdiction.

    The moment that the trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, was planned, commentators began comparing it to the 1945 Yalta Conference. Unsurprisingly, this narrative was particularly fueled by Moscow, where the British-Soviet-U.S. “Massive Three” summit stands for the codification of Soviet control over half of Europe. Pyotr Tolstoy, the head of the foreign affairs committee in the Russian parliament, called the summit a “newly introduced Yalta.” Ultranationalist ideologue Alexander Dugin found the meeting “deeply symbolic,” while the Kremlin boasted that “the significance and symbolism of this meeting are hard to overestimate.”.

    Sources indicate that the Kremlin was right about the symbolism, not least because this week’s summit produced little else. The joint “Declaration Toward Peace” adopted by U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin notes practically nothing. It pledges United Nations reform without specifics, future fuel shipments without volumes or deadlines, and a dialogue on nuclear risks without a clear path forward. Its most pointed passage is a warning to the International Criminal Court not to abuse its jurisdiction.

    In a recent development, nothing about this is surprising. The vagueness on arms control reflects China’s lack of interest in it amid a rapid build-out of its nuclear forces. Ukraine is not mentioned, because Russia has made it repeatedly clear that it is not ready for peace in Europe on anything but its maximalist demands. Iran, too, was absent from the agenda, given Russian and Chinese support for Iran and the embarrassing cul-de-sac that the war represents for Trump.

    Sources indicate that but substance was hardly the point. The mere image of the three leaders sitting together made the summit significant—and made capitals from Taipei to Kyiv to Tokyo nervous that the three might strike a private understanding over their heads.

    To understand what yesterday’s summit really meant, Yalta is indeed a useful comparison—but mainly for the differences that it reveals.

    According to recent reports, the first is the diminished stature of today’s threesome. The Major Three met as the victors of a war that had left much of Europe and Asia in ruins. What they decided at Yalta—and at the Potsdam Conference a few months later—drew lines that would last for more than four decades. The three leaders who met in Shenzhen are weak, each in his own way, and each of them needed a photo-op to project a strength that he does not fully possess.

    Sources indicate that china was not invited to Yalta because it was on the menu: U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin agreed on Soviet rights over the Manchurian railways and ports of Dairen and Port Arthur without consulting the Republic of China’s leader, Chiang Kai-shek.

    It has been revealed that eighty-one years later, a different China was the host. The location was carefully chosen: In 1980, when it became China’s first special economic zone, Shenzhen was a small town across the border from Hong Kong, whereas today it is one of the world’s leading technology and manufacturing hubs. But the rise that Shenzhen embodies is losing pace. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) expects Chinese economic growth to slow to 4.5 percent this year and 4 percent in 2027 as weak domestic demand and a real estate crisis weigh on the economy. Demographic decline will shrink the country’s population by 786 million by 2100. The flashy summit was also a way to distract the world from the change in China’s trajectory.

    For Putin, the gain of face was even greater, given that by any material measure, Russia plays in a much smaller league. The IMF projects the U.S. GDP at $32.6 trillion in 2026 and China’s at $21.5 trillion. Russia’s is only about $2.7 trillion, roughly the size of Italy’s. Military spending tells the same story. In 2025, the United States spent $954 billion, China an estimated $336 billion, and Russia $190 billion. European NATO members together spent $559 billion, almost three times as much as Russia.

    Putin’s seat in Shenzhen was therefore the dividend of nearly two decades of growing, calculated aggressiveness. Georgia, Syria, the 2014 and 2022 invasions of Ukraine, and the current hybrid attacks across Europe are a sequence of moves resting on the same bet. Moscow has converted Europe’s passivity into status, compensating for what it lacks in economic and military weight with a willingness to use force that none of its rivals share.

    Industry observers note that the bet paid off because Europe preferred to ignore the implications. Germany shrugged off Russia’s 2014 invasion of Crimea and the Donbas and moved forward with Nord Stream 2, thereby entrenching the continent’s energy dependence on Moscow. Since 2022, Europe has financed Ukraine’s defense without ever resolving to push for Kyiv’s victory. And Washington bears its share in encouraging Putin, from former President Barack Obama’s impotent red line in Syria in 2013 to Trump granting Moscow sanctions relief and a seat among the great powers before any settlement of Russia’s war.

    For Trump, the summit was a welcome respite from a string of setbacks. On Nov. 3, Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, winning various Republican strongholds for the first time in generations. The botched attack on Iran contributed to this electoral punishment, not least through its impact on gas prices.

    According to recent reports, add to this that Trump has never hidden his admiration for leaders who govern without democratic constraints. A seat at the table with two of them, with all the ceremony that came with it, was worth a great deal to a president facing a hostile Congress and having few foreign successes to show for the year. “It’s a big win for us,” he told reporters as the meeting opened.

    The strategic environment could hardly be more different from 1945. The leaders who met then were looking to consolidate the status quo that had emerged from the war, which they all found acceptable. By contrast, the three powers that met in Shenzhen are, each in its own way, fundamentally revisionist.

    China has its sights on Taiwan and wresting technological leadership from the United States. Russia has its war in Europe and a relationship with Beijing that becomes more lopsided every year. The United States is renegotiating its alliances and trade policy while stuck in a quagmire in Iran. The U.S.-China trade truce expires in January, and the Nvidia scandal indicates how far the technology rivalry now reaches. All three are navigating a strategic environment in flux, which each sees as an intermediate stop to improve its own position.

    The third and deepest difference is vividly depicted by Europe’s absence. At Yalta, Europe sat among the victors. France, following four years under German occupation and the collaborationist Vichy regime, was of course not invited. For Poland and much of Central Europe, the conference is a reminder of a settlement imposed at its expense. But British Prime Minister Winston Churchill spoke for a European power that had fought the war since 1939—and the order that he helped design, from the postwar occupation of Germany to the creation of the United Nations, was one with freedom at its very core.

    Sources indicate that in Shenzhen, no European leader was in the room, the visible outcome of decades of strategic decline. The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a forum of 21 Pacific Rim economies of which no European Union member state is a member.

    It has been revealed that in fact, each of the three leaders at the table is, in different ways, working against Europe. China does it through trade: In 2025, the EU ran a deficit of 359.8 billion euros with China; the largest category of imports was mechanical appliances, electrical machinery, and equipment, the industrial core that Europe is trying to protect.

    Russia does it through force: Its war against Ukraine is in its fifth year, and its hybrid campaign of sabotage, drone incursions, disinformation, and intimidation now reaches deep into EU territory.

    Recent findings suggest that the United States does it through ideological disdain, made crystal clear by Vice President J.D. Vance’s speech at the 2025 Munich Security Conference and by a National Security Strategy that warned of Europe’s “civilizational erasure” and committed Washington to supporting “patriotic” (read: far-right) parties on the continent, on top of tariffs on European goods at levels unseen in the postwar trans-Atlantic relationship.

    This genuinely anti-European stance was the only real common denominator in Shenzhen—a hostility fueled by Europe’s weakness, to be sure, but even more by a shared ideology of power. Yalta was a meeting of champions of different worldviews. Roosevelt and Churchill embodied the liberal democracies that were about to defeat Nazism. Stalin embodied a revolutionary state with a rival vision of political and economic order and ultimately of humanity itself. Within three years, this ideological divergence would harden into the Cold War. For all its ill effects on the nations caught on the Soviet side, Yalta is still an icon of pragmatism across an ideological divide.

    It has been revealed that shenzhen was the exact opposite. The three leaders do not lack conflicting interests. Washington wants Beijing in a trilateral arms control framework that the Chinese Foreign Ministry calls “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic.” The United States is at war with Iran, and the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz hits China’s energy supplies. Russia and China are far from strategic allies, and diplomatic protocol in Shenzhen showed how unequal their relationship has become.

    But on the question that divided the room at Yalta—namely, how power should be constrained and legitimized—the three leaders in Shenzhen are closer to one another than any of them is to almost every other leader across the world. All three think of sovereignty as the right of strong states to act without external constraint. All three read the world in terms of spheres of influence and privilege bilateral deals to multilateral rules.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, all three regard checks and balances, independent courts, and a free press as nuisances and obstacles at home and abroad. It is telling that one of the four points of their declaration—and the only one that wasn’t lukewarm boilerplate—defends the immunity of state officials and warns the International Criminal Court against abusing its jurisdiction.

    In this sense, all three are anti-Western in the deepest sense of the term. For Xi and Putin, rejecting the underlying idea of the West is long-standing doctrine, but the United States—the country that once defined and defended the West—now shares much of the same inclination.

    It has been revealed that this is how the world has changed since 1945. At Yalta, ideological opposites negotiated a balance of power. In Shenzhen, three leaders with a shared worldview but competing interests discussed the affairs of the world, producing symbolism rather than substance. The two superpowers and their Russian sidekick were in a bubble, with neither the West nor anyone else represented in the room.

    For all the lack of substance, that may be the summit’s most important outcome: If what we saw this week portends a lasting realignment of the United States, this summit’s legacy could be far greater than the one to which it was so eagerly compared.

    Three Routes to VPP Revenue for Installers, EPCs, and Developers Utility programs, wholesale markets, and bilateral contracts each come with different eligibility rules, payment structures, and commercial responsibilities.

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that in June 2026, Google and Voltus revealed a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM.
    • Industry observers note that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs.
    • In a recent development, utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Intersolar & Energy Storage North America.

    It has been revealed that in June 2026, Google and Voltus revealed a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM. Under Voltus’s Bring Your Own Capacity model, Google funds procurement while Voltus aggregates qualifying distributed energy resources (DERs) and compensates participating customers.1.

    Industry observers note that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs. Across the U.S., utility programs, wholesale electricity markets, and bilateral contracts each have their own eligibility requirements, payment structures and commercial responsibilities.

    Utility programs and procurement.

    In a recent development, utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need. Payments may be tied to enrollment, committed capacity, measured performance or a combination of these factors. Massachusetts, for example, offers residential battery customers $275 per kW of average summer performance through ConnectedSolutions2.

    Beyond customer incentive programs, utilities also procure distributed flexibility through contracts to address local grid constraints or broader capacity needs. Unlike standardized incentives, these arrangements can establish specific delivery requirements and compensation terms, creating opportunities for developers and service providers to assemble and manage DER portfolios. During a July 2026 heat event, Green Mountain Power dispatched 90 MW of stored energy capacity, helping customers avoid an estimated $6 million in peak-related costs during one peak hour3.

    Sources indicate that aggregated DERs can earn revenue from energy, capacity, and ancillary services in wholesale electricity markets, subject to regional market rules and resource qualification. Unlike utility-specific programs, wholesale markets can provide access to broader regional revenue opportunities and multiple grid services. For developers and installers, participation typically occurs through an aggregator or other qualified market participant rather than through direct market registration.

    In a recent development, while Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 2222 established a broader framework for DER participation, uneven implementation across regional markets continues to constrain commercial opportunities for aggregated resources. Market access does not automatically translate into revenue, as individual resources must still meet qualification requirements and comply with market-specific rules. New York Independent System Operator (NYISO), for example, requires DER aggregations to meet minimum capacity and real-time telemetry requirements, which can increase participation costs and limit the economic viability of smaller resources.

    Recent findings suggest that wholesale participation can also expose VPP portfolios to fluctuating market prices, performance obligations and restrictions on receiving compensation for overlapping services. In Texas, ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) pilot allows aggregated DERs to participate in wholesale energy and ancillary services markets, subject to qualification, telemetry, and dispatch requirements.

    Bilateral contracts and emerging buyers.

    Recent findings suggest that bilateral contracts allow utilities and large electricity consumers to procure distributed flexibility directly from aggregators and service providers. Growing interest from data center operators and other large energy buyers is expanding the potential market for VPP capacity beyond traditional utility programs. Unlike standardized programs, bilateral agreements can be tailored to a buyer’s specific needs, with negotiated terms for capacity, delivery periods, compensation, and performance obligations.

    Industry observers note that the appropriate route depends on existing customer relationships, market access, and the responsibilities each partner assumes. Developers and EPCs working on commercial storage projects may find opportunities through utility procurement or capacity contracts, while residential installers with established battery customer bases may be well positioned to incorporate VPP enrollment into utility programs. Wholesale markets can expand revenue opportunities through aggregation partners, and bilateral contracts can create opportunities to develop resources around specific buyer needs.

    #168289. The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2281 w)

    The Fantasy of a Turkish Middle East

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.
    • Since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested.
    • Turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    MELIHA BENLI ALTUNISIK is Professor of International Relations at Middle East Technical University.

    Ankara’s Risky Bid to Impose Regional Order.

    Since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, the future of the Middle East has been fiercely contested. The previous Gulf-centered order had Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) trying to stabilize and shape the region using economic statecraft and the normalization of relations with former foes in Iran, Israel, Turkey, and Syria. Three years of war in Gaza, and more recently in Iran and the Gulf, have severely disrupted that order-building project and generated a deep sense of uncertainty about what comes next.

    Turkey, like every major power in the Middle East, has tried to fill the vacuum. Before 2023, Ankara’s influence had been in decline; after years of diplomatic isolation following the Arab uprisings, it had just begun repairing its ties with major regional actors. But in the past few years, Turkey has earned American backing for its policies in Syria and its regional diplomacy, and it has made an effort to secure the home front by pursuing a peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), a militant group that has fought a decades-long insurgency against the Turkish state. Most recently, in August, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey signed the Mecca Defense Alliance, a collective security agreement that institutionalizes Turkey’s regional positioning and pulls the country directly into Saudi Arabia’s war with the Houthis.

    Recent findings suggest that turkey’s post–October 7 strategy has restored the country’s position as a regional heavyweight. But it is not capable of meeting its larger objective: establishing order on its own terms. Turkey, like the region’s other aspiring leaders, lacks the power to impose a new security framework on its own. Its nascent efforts to build one, such as the new Mecca pact, merely make countries outside the bloc feel unsafe, feeding instability. Turkey’s most ambitious plays for regional leadership are therefore likely to prove ineffective or even counterproductive. As long as the Middle East’s highly militarized, zero-sum security dynamics remain, Ankara would be better off concentrating on interests closer to home that it has the power to protect.

    Recent findings suggest that this is not the first time that Turkey has tried to shape the broader Middle Eastern order. Ankara saw the Arab uprisings in the early 2010s as a historic window of opportunity. The ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) described the political transformation sweeping the region as “the people’s coming to power,” and the Turkish government expected that eventual elections in the Arab countries rocked by protest would bring into office parties aligned with the Muslim Brotherhood, which was ideologically sympathetic and had practical links to the AKP. The emergence of friendly governments, the thinking went, would increase Turkey’s influence in the region.

    In a recent development, yet these hopes soon receded. Egypt’s Muslim Brotherhood–affiliated president, Mohamed Morsi, was overthrown in 2013, and Turkey’s bet on the opposition movement in Syria failed as Bashar al-Assad clung to power. Turkey was left isolated. A rival axis composed of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE objected to Turkey’s Muslim Brotherhood ties and sought to limit Ankara’s influence. This group contested Turkey’s positions across the Middle East, North Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, and the Horn of Africa, effectively fighting proxy battles with Turkey in conflicts in Libya, Somalia, and Syria.

    Then, the attacks on October 7, 2023, ushered in another period of upheaval. Some changes since have played in Turkey’s favor. Chief among them is the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria in December 2024 at the hands of opposition groups led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham. Turkey had arguably invested more than any other country in pursuit of regime change in Damascus; it assisted opposition groups for years. Yet as the years went by, that objective seemed increasingly out of reach. The region’s other major powers made their peace with the regime’s survival, and even Ankara began considering rapprochement with Assad to avoid being left out in the cold. Assad’s fall changed Turkey’s fortunes overnight, handing it a level of influence in Syria it had not held in more than a decade.

    In a recent development, other developments proved more dangerous for Ankara. Israel’s foreign policy became more assertive and revisionist after October 7, and its expansive security objectives began to clash with Turkey’s own. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s sharp criticism of Israeli policies in Gaza strained the relationship, and it deteriorated further when Turkey expanded its foothold in post-Assad Syria and Israel came to view Ankara’s military presence there as a direct threat. As Israel continues to strike sites in Syria—attacks Ankara has condemned—the risk of escalation is only growing. A miscalculation on either side could lead to a direct clash between Israeli and Turkish forces.

    It has been revealed that the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, meanwhile, has cut both ways for Turkey. While Tehran’s attention has been focused elsewhere, Ankara has welcomed Iran’s retreat from Syria and the chance to push back against its remaining influence in Iraq. Turkey also has no interest in seeing a nuclear-armed Iran upend the regional balance of power. Yet the prospect of chaos across Turkey’s eastern border, should the Iranian regime fall, has bred real anxiety in Ankara, as has the possibility that Iran could become emboldened if the regime emerges from the war intact.

    Recent findings suggest that in this complex environment, Ankara has pursued a three-pronged strategy to protect its security interests and, it hopes, capitalize on opportunities the upheaval has created. Since U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to power, Erdogan has drawn Turkey closer to the United States and tried to use his relationship with Washington to advance Ankara’s regional policies. Turkey has also pressed ahead with regional normalization, building on efforts to repair ties with Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other key Arab countries in the early 2020s, with the aim to forge a broader regional bloc. And, domestically, Ankara launched the “Turkey Without Terror” process, an attempt to resolve the conflict with the PKK inside and outside Turkey, which Turkey’s adversaries have long exploited by arming Kurdish groups or backing them politically.

    Some of Ankara’s policies have borne fruit. Consider, for instance, the outreach to Washington. Erdogan’s close relations with Trump helped bring the United States on board with Turkey’s expanded role in Syria. Turkey was one of the four countries Washington brought in to help negotiate the U.S.-proposed October 2025 cease-fire agreement between Israel and Hamas, and as a result, Trump offered and Erdogan accepted a seat on the U.S. president’s so-called Board of Peace for Gaza’s reconstruction. Turkey has played an active part mediating between the United States and Iran during the latest war. And Trump publicly endorsed the Mecca Defense Alliance, calling it “big, bold, and crucial.” All of this points to a recognition in Washington of Turkey’s regional importance, the U.S. administration’s willingness to support some of Ankara’s priorities, and Turkey’s determination to elevate its own position.

    Industry observers note that yet there are undeniable limits to Turkey’s quest for influence. At a February 2026 Board of Peace summit, for instance, Turkey was excluded from participating in a planned international troop deployment and police training in Gaza—a sign that warming relations with Washington were not enough to override Israeli objections to having a Turkish military footprint in the Palestinian territory. In Syria, similarly, the support Turkey has secured from the Trump administration has not stopped Israel from launching military strikes at Syrian targets near Turkish positions. Simply put, Turkey has not been able to use its relationship with the Trump administration to overcome the limit Israeli opposition places on the scope of Turkey’s regional role.

    Industry observers note that turkey’s regional normalization efforts have yielded mixed results, too. Restoring diplomatic ties with significant players such as Saudi Arabia is in Turkey’s interest, to be sure. But the alliances Ankara is entering with these countries risk making Turkey and the region less secure, not more. The Mecca pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia could end up hardening rival blocs and elevating regional tensions. Turkey insists that the alliance is directed against no country in particular and has suggested that Egypt, Syria, or even Iran could eventually join. But in the meantime, Iran, Israel, and the Houthis could see it as a threat and try to test or weaken its members’ commitment.

    Furthermore, the pact could pull Turkey into other countries’ wars. That possibility is already on the table now that the Turkish parliament has ratified the agreement and the Houthis are escalating their attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Turkish government has insisted that any military support it provided would be confined to deterrence, intelligence sharing, and defense-industrial cooperation. Yet Saudi Arabia is now seeking Pakistan’s and Turkey’s help with air defense and territorial protection, and the three states have agreed to prepare forces for rapid deployment. Sending Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia would still require separate parliamentary approval. If parliament allowed it, even a limited deployment would risk drawing Turkey into a wider regional conflict.

    Recent findings suggest that some kind of regional security framework is necessary. The problem is that no country in the region, including Turkey, has the power to impose a security order on the rest, so whenever someone tries, other countries feel threatened. An informal cooperation framework that is open to all countries in the region—and that asks its members to commit to nonaggression instead of making mutual-defense pledges—might work better. But the assembly and functioning of such a coalition require trust that governments in the region do not have. Breaking the impasse would likely require the United States to play a more constructive role than it has in recent years—not simply endorsing whatever regional arrangement emerges, as Trump did with the Mecca pact, or pressuring countries to normalize relations with Israel without expecting Israel to change its policies in return, as Trump has also done. Instead, Washington, perhaps with the help of Beijing, would need to compel regional rivals such as Iran and Saudi Arabia to take confidence-building measures that would make an inclusive security framework viable in the long run. Without this external push, the narrower security blocs that emerge in the region will only lead to further instability.

    In a recent development, ankara’s strongest cards lie closer to home. The Kurdish peace process has moved slowly since February 2025, when Abdullah Ocalan, the imprisoned leader of the PKK, called on the militant group to disarm. But it has yielded tangible progress. In May 2025, the PKK announced that it would dissolve. In Syria, Kurdish forces are being integrated into the Syrian army, and Mazloum Abdi, the commander of the People’s Defense Units, a Kurdish armed group affiliated with the PKK, was appointed as a presidential adviser in August. Syria’s postconflict transition remains fragile, and the reconciliation between Damascus and Kurdish militants in the northeast may owe as much to American pressure as it does to Turkey’s domestic efforts to make peace with the PKK. But for Turkey, the eventual integration of Syrian Kurdish forces into the Syrian state removes the risk Ankara saw in having an autonomous, armed Kurdish entity on its southern border. And, given the close security and economic ties Ankara has developed with Damascus, as well as the political and legal steps the government can take at home to complete the disbanding of the PKK and to deepen democratic reforms, Turkey has the ability to keep these encouraging developments on track.

    It has been revealed that turkey’s regional policies are most successful when the country plays to its strengths—not when it is trying to throw its weight around the region. In the first decade of the twenty-first century, Ankara built real influence by mediating between Syria and Israel and between Palestinian factions, expanding its economic engagement in the Levant, and proposing projects to connect the region’s energy and transportation infrastructure. Military power, meanwhile, has proved most effective when applied for specific purposes, such as to secure the border with Syria. This combination is Turkey’s winning formula: diplomacy and economic outreach to extend its influence, and limited force to protect its core interests. Broad, open-ended commitments, by contrast, risk drawing Turkey into regional conflicts without making it safer.

    Today, sticking to a more effective formula does not mean retreating from regional politics. It means setting priorities and planning long-term. Consolidating the Kurdish peace process, keeping Washington invested in Syria’s stabilization, managing the risk of confrontation with Israel in Syria, and maintaining constructive relations with the Kurdistan Regional Government in northern Iraq and the Iraqi government in Baghdad are key to keeping Turkey’s borders secure and are within Turkey’s ability to achieve. Ankara can continue to use its experience in mediation when opportunities to advance peace processes present themselves. It can also promote economic connectivity, both by expanding trade ties and by supporting regional infrastructure projects such as the Iraq-Europe Development Road and a proposed pipeline network connecting the Gulf to Jordan, Syria, and Turkey. It need not shy away from security cooperation with the Gulf, either, if it can engage without making formal commitments. Yet in all these endeavors, Ankara should remember that it has the most clout when it stays out of the region’s conflicts.

    Industry observers note that the Middle East’s escalating wars and rival blocs could make a narrower Turkish security policy more difficult to sustain today than it was in the past. Defending Ankara’s interests and playing a constructive role in a volatile neighborhood will require a careful balance. The best way Turkey can contribute to regional stability may be to avoid trying to do too much.

    Why BAAJA Matters

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
